title: Risk of terror attack on Maldives resort is high
abstract: Subject Political instability and militant threat in the Maldives. Significance Maldivian President Abdulla Yameen in July ordered the military to lock down the country’s parliament, obstructing a no-confidence vote in the speaker that would have undermined Yameen’s control of the legislature. Around 200 Maldivian militants are thought to have travelled to Iraq and Syria in recent years. The Maldives economy is heavily dependent on tourism. Impacts Yameen may use the judiciary to bolster executive control. Saudi Arabia may increase financing for constructing mosques and training clerics. China may step up efforts to acquire an island for military development. Any attack on a tourist resort may prompt capital flight from private Indian investors.

title: China's Expansion to Eurasia as a "Fate-Changer": For Better or Worse?
abstract: China's Expansion to Eurasia as a "Fate-Changer":For Better or Worse? Nargis Kassenova (bio) Daniel Markey's China's Western Horizon: Beijing and the New Geopolitics of Eurasia is an excellent and extremely timely study of China's growing engagement in South Asia, Central Asia, and the Middle East. It addresses the need to better understand current developments in Eurasia and consider the options and implications for U.S. policy. The book has multiple strengths. A geographic scope comprising three regions allows for good optics and perspective levels. The author makes granular analyses of developments on the ground in both domestic and regional political contexts and compares and generalizes findings into broader stroke geopolitical assessments. This helps avoid the pitfalls of preconceptions and superficiality that are typical of the grand strategy genre. Central Asia—generally less in the limelight and less-studied than other regions—tends to suffer in particular from this mistreatment. Another of the book's strengths is its accounting for individual agency that skillfully incorporates statements and opinions of policymakers and experts. This inclusion of many voices, ranging from purposeful rhetoric to anonymous reflections shared with the author during interviews in the United States, China, Russia, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, and Israel, enriches the narrative and conveys the nuances of the complex politics of the different regions. Markey draws attention to the role of digital infrastructure that, along with energy and transportation infrastructure, has become a pillar of cooperation between China and its partners under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) umbrella. He rightly emphasizes that "to be influential, China's involvement in other states does not need to take the shape of old-fashioned empire or even modern investments in roads, railways and ports," and that "in this century, information and telecommunications networks—and their supporting hardware, software, and standards—are also potent sources of power" (pp. 3–4). The book also discusses the new Chinese-built overland fiber-optic network connecting China and Pakistan to service all of Pakistan, as well as Iran's import of surveillance technologies [End Page 143] from ZTE and the commission of its National Information Network data centers to Huawei. Over the past several years, Chinese information and communications technology companies and their digital technologies also have made inroads in Kazakhstan and Saudi Arabia that are not mentioned in the book. While China's Digital Silk Road is a hot topic, developments in specific regions are generally still underexplored and there is clearly room for further study.1 In the book's comparative analysis of national responses to BRI by Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Iran, and Saudi Arabia, I was struck by their similarity and synchronicity. In 2015, Pakistan's Ministry of Planning, Development and Reform adopted the "Ascending the Saga of National Progress" document envisioning the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor as a "'fate-changer for Pakistan'" (p. 48). It included a comprehensive package of cooperative initiatives and projects, covering key areas including connectivity, information, network infrastructure, energy cooperation, industries and industrial parks, agricultural development, poverty alleviation, tourism, financial cooperation, and livelihood improvement via municipal infrastructure, education, public health, and people-to-people communication. The same year, Kazakhstan launched its new economic policy, Nurly Zhol (Bright Path), that aimed at investing $9 billion in domestic transportation and logistics, energy, and industrial and public utilities infrastructure—and agreed with China to develop a plan for linking it with BRI. In 2016, Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman announced the ambitious Vision 2030, envisaging the expansion of non-energy industries, including manufacturing, technology, and tourism, and turning the kingdom into a competitive hub for global trade and transit. From the very beginning, China has been seen as a major partner for implementing Vision 2030. All three governments established committees with Chinese counterparts to link and harmonize their development plans. This official alignment of national development strategies and ambitions with those of Beijing is an important phenomenon: the appeal of the Chinese model and the all-around veneration of infrastructure are at the core of China's global soft power. It remains to be seen what will happen if these national infrastructure and connectivity-focused plans fail or result in unintended consequences. [End Page 144...

title: Baromètre OMT du tourisme mondial et annexe statistique, juillet 2021
abstract: Seuls les principaux chapitres de la publication ont été traduits. Le reste de la publication figure dans la langue originale (Anglais). International travel largely on hold despite uptick in May 2021 International tourist arrivals (overnight visitors) dropped by 85% in January-May 2021 compared to the same period of pre-pandemic year 2019, or 65% over 2020, as travel restrictions remained high due to the coronavirus pandemic. This follows an unprecedented drop of 73% in 2020, the worst year on record for international tourism This sharp decline represents a loss of some 147 million international arrivals compared to the same five months of 2020, or 460 million compared to 2019. By regions, Asia and the Pacific continued to suffer the largest decline with a 95% drop in international arrivals in the first five months of 2021 over the same period in 2019. Europe (-85%) recorded the second largest decline in arrivals, followed by the Middle East (-83%) and Africa (-81%). The Americas (-72%) saw a comparatively smaller decrease. Despite the weak results, international tourism saw a minor uptick in May 2021 with arrivals declining by 82% (versus May 2019), after falling by 86% in April, as some destinations started to ease travel restrictions and consumer confidence rose slightly. After an estimated 64% plunge in international tourism receipts in 2020, destinations continued to report very weak revenues in the first five months of 2021, ranging from 50% to 90% declines compared to 2019. However, several countries recorded a small uptick in the month of May following a minor improvement in international arrivals. In terms of outbound travel among the top 20 source markets, Saudi Arabia (-42%) and Belgium (-46%) saw relatively better results in January-May 2021, as well as the Republic of Korea, Malaysia and Switzerland, all recording 50% declines in international tourism expenditure compared to the same period in 2019. France is also worth noting, with -54% in expenditure compared to 2019. International travel is slowly picking up from very low levels, though the recovery remains fragile and uneven amid much uncertainty. Domestic travel is driving the recovery of tourism in several destinations, especially those with large domestic markets. Domestic air seat capacity in China and Russia has already exceeded pre-crisis levels. Along with the ongoing vaccination roll-out, the safe and responsible restart of tourism will continue to depend on a coordinated response among countries regarding travel restrictions, harmonized safety protocols and effective communication to help restore consumer confidence.

title: Geografias do mundo imaginário
abstract: Geographies of the imagined world. The idea that Geography ismore about the construction of images of the world than about a given “objective reality” inspired this study of the mental representations of several countries. Among the multiple possible representations of 12 countries (Portugal, France, Norway, Egypt,Mauritania, Mozambique, United States, Mexico, Brazil, China, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia), we began by charting their location in a world map as indicated by over 300 respondents with at least high school attendance. Then, the compilation of a vast number of mental images (three per country and respondent) led to the definition ofsix general categories that bring together mental images of a similar kind: nature, culture and history, tourism and gastronomy, economy and society, specific places and no answer/wrong answers. In each category, we have highlighted the dominant (most frequent)idea. Location, the relative frequency of the no answer/wrong answerscategory and the dominant images for each country all proved significant when it comes to dividing the countries into groups, and serve as indicators of the richness and variety of the mental representations. The study provided answers to some of the original research questions, but leaves many others unanswered.

title: Green Hospitality 2030: Enhancing Guest Experience through Sustainable Innovation and the European Green Deal
abstract: This paper explores the evolution of academic research in green hospitality, with a focus on how sustainability, innovation, and guest experience converge under the guiding framework of the European Green Deal (EGD). Through a bibliometric analysis of 181 peer-reviewed articles published between 2019 and 2025 and indexed in the Scopus database, the study provides a comprehensive overview of global research trends in sustainable hospitality. Using VOSviewer and Biblioshiny, the analysis identified key thematic clusters—sustainability, hotel industry, and corporate social responsibility—alongside the most prolific countries, authors, and journals contributing to the field. The United States, China, Saudi Arabia, India, and the United Kingdom emerged as top contributors, while Sustainability (Switzerland) and the International Journal of Hospitality Management were highlighted as leading publication sources. Authors such as Han, who has focused extensively on green consumer behavior and sustainable tourism decisionmaking, Fayyad, recognized for his work on strategic sustainability practices in hospitality, and Azazz, noted for his contributions to green marketing and authenticity in hotels, were recognized for their influential work. The findings reveal a growing academic and industry-wide interest in integrating green practices and innovative strategies to enhance guest experience and operational performance. This research is one of the few to systematically align bibliometric insights with the priorities of the EGD, thereby adding original value to both academic literature and practical decision-making. The study’s results offer meaningful guidance for hospitality managers, policymakers, and researchers by identifying strategic areas for investment and collaboration in sustainable innovation. It underscores the importance of aligning green practices with guest satisfaction and long-term value creation in the hospitality sector.

title: Editorial: Community series in mental illness, culture, and society: dealing with the COVID-19 pandemic, volume VIII
abstract: them, Xu and colleagues evaluated the mental health status of community frontline medical workers after the normalized management of COVID-19 in Sichuan, China (18). Along the same lines, the study conducted by Schaffler et al. tried to explore burdens, resources, and determinants of good or poor well-being among Austrian psychotherapists (19). Büssing and Baumann focused on the experience of loss and grief among people from Germany who lost their relatives during the pandemic, with a reflection on the impact of the support provided by healthcare professionals (20). Through a longitudinal study design, Lureiro and her team also studied the Brazilian healthcare workers' emotional burden and the effects on professional fulfillment at the end of the third wave of COVID-19 (21). Fatima and colleagues conducted an in-depth analysis of the moral injury among healthcare providers in Pakistan during the pandemic (22). Ieng Lam et al. launched a national survey in China to study the prevalence of COVID-19 fear and its association with quality of life and network structure among Chinese mental health professionals after ending China's dynamic zero-COVID policy (23). On the other hand, in another survey study in China, the group led by Feng explored the workload change and depression among emergency medical staff after the open policy during the pandemic (24). A qualitative cross-sectional analysis by imagery in scientific literature and its use for people working in the German healthcare sector (25). In another survey, Vaillant-Ciszewicz and colleagues studied the psychological impact of the first lockdown on French nursing homes, particularly the impact on psychologists, psychomotors therapists, and occupational therapists (26). Wang et al. managed a large-scale cross-sectional study about the prevalence of anxiety and associated factors among frontline nurses following the pandemic in China (27). Still, the work by Sanchez-Plazas et al. highlights the psychological impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on physicians in Puerto Rico (28). Finally, the last paper in this specific sub-topic emanates from Józef Nowicki et al., who focused on the relationship between the strength of religious faith and spirituality with post-traumatic growth among nurses caring for patients with COVID-19 in eastern Poland (29).Many articles discussed the impact of COVID-19 on students, trainees, and residents. In this regard, the study by Rahman Ashiq et al. reported on the levels of depression, anxiety, stress, and fear of COVID-19 among Bangladeshi medical students during the first wave of the pandemic in the country (30). The group led by Mulatie Anteneh in Ethiopia focused on the psychological impact of the pandemic and associated factors among college and university students in 2022 (31).The paper by Atasha Serrano et al. explored sociodemographic characteristics, social support, and family history as risk factors for depression, anxiety, and stress among young adult senior high school students in the Philippines (32). Alternatively, Wei and colleagues evaluated the current status of e-learning, personality traits, and coping styles among medical students during the pandemic (33). Cerbino and Portero de la Cruz wrote a piece about the psychological impact of COVID-19 and its determinants among Spanish university students (34). Zhang et al. wanted to better understand which psychological status and related factors of resident physicians were more relevant during the release of COVID-19 pandemic restrictions in China (35). In the article by Rahgozar and Giménez-Llort, findings highlight the design and effectiveness of an online group logotherapy intervention on the mental health of Iranian international students residing in European countries during the pandemic (36). Ding and collaborators published a paper about the prospective associations between time management tendency, negative emotions, and problematic smartphone use among Chinese nursing students (37). Still, Wagner and colleagues studied mental distress, food insecurity, and university student dropout during the COVID-19 pandemic in South Africa (38). Finally, the last paper in this subtopic emerges from Fu et al. who validated a scale evaluating multicultural personality traits of Chinese university students and their effects on psychological adjustment in the aftermath of COVID-19 in Shanghai (39).The richest group of articles is that of 15 manuscripts that discuss special, fragile, or minority populations during the pandemic. Usher et al. explored the relationship between mental health and the use of medicare benefits follow-up mental health services by Indigenous people in Australia during COVID-19 (40). Furthermore, the team led by Busili studied COVID-19 exposure and depression-anxiety levels among Saudi adults in the Jazan region, in a sample size predominantly made up of female and undergraduate individuals (41). Steinhausen-Wachowsky and colleagues evaluated the stability of psychological well-being during the pandemic among people with an anthroposophical worldview, with a specific reflection on the influence of wondering awe and perception of nature as resources (42) (48). Again from South Korea, Kim and colleagues examined the relationship between sleep quality and depressive symptoms in women engaged in soccer (49). A four-year prospective study run in Taiwan by Huang et al. evaluated the predictive effects of prepandemic sexual stigma, affective symptoms, and family support on the fear from COVID-19 among lesbian, gay, and bisexual individuals (50). Bühler and Willmund investigated, during the third wave of the pandemic, the deployment-related quarantining as a risk or resilience factor for German military service members (51). The study led by Liu estimated the prevalence of COVID-19 fear and its association with quality of life among fire service recruits after ceasing the dynamic zero-COVID policy (52). Dones and Ciobanu studied the older adults' experiences of wellbeing during the pandemic in a comparative qualitative study design, with a peculiar focus on coping mechanisms in Italy and Switzerland (53). Lastly, Wei et al. estimated the prevalence of depressive symptoms and its correlates among individuals in China who self-reported SARS-CoV-2 infection after optimizing the COVID-19 response (54).Nine studies were conducted in specific locations or areas. Among them, in Japan Saito et al. studied the age group differences in psychological distress and leisure-time exercise/socioeconomic status during the pandemic (55). Krawczyk-Suszek and Kleinrok published a paper on the quality of life of a healthy Polish population in association with specific sociodemographic factors during COVID-19 (56). Moya-Salazar et al. ran a systematic review tackling the mental health situation in rural Andean populations in Latin America during the pandemic (57). Abdel-Rahman and colleagues proposed a series of predictors of mental health issues during the outbreak in Egypt, mainly highlighting food security, incomes, and livelihoods (58). In a Mendelian randomization study, Xue et al. investigated the susceptibility and severity of COVID-19 and the risk of psychiatric disorders in European populations (59). Sik Chu and Lee conducted a propensity score matching analysis on depressive symptoms among people under COVID-19 quarantine or self-isolation in South Korea (60). In a study from Saudi Arabia, Al-Johani et al. evaluated post-COVID-19 fatigue and health-related quality of life in the general population (61). Zenba et al. published a paper in Japan on psychological distress among older adults due to fear from COVID-19, mainly via lifestyle disruption and leisure restriction (62).Finally, Fernandes and his team studied stress, anxiety, and depression trajectories during the first wave in Portugal, through some drives such as resilient, adaptive, and maladaptive responses (63).Four studies about specific treatments or home therapies were included in this volume. In particular, the work by Moreno-Alonso et al. analyzed patients' satisfaction and outcomes of crisis resolution home treatment for the management of acute psychiatric crises during the COVID-19 pandemic in Madrid (64). Sandra and colleagues proposed a peculiar pilot study to apply a twoweek home exercise program targeting depressive symptoms in the coronavirus crisis context (65).On the other hand, Jiang et al. published a paper including a multidimensional comparative analysis of help-seeking messages during different stages of the pandemic in China (66). Finally, Luo et al. discussed the role of diverse forms of art therapy as potentially effective treatment measures for psychiatric symptoms in patients with COVID-19 (67).Three papers discussed pharmacoeconomics and politics during the pandemic. He and colleagues studied the potential link between the relaxation of the COVID-19 control policy and residents' mental health, in view of the mediating role of family tourism consumption in China (68). In the article by Sarasjärvi et al., the behavioral patterns Western Australians during and after lockdown were analyzed (69). Lastly, the team led by Stojkovic presented a brief report on the impact of the pandemic on the prescription trend of long-acting injections of paliperidone and risperidone in Serbia (70).Two articles dealt with the theme of suicide. Jeremic et al. assessed whether the trend of suicide by self-immolation among a sample of adolescents may have undergone significant changes due to COVID-19 (71). alternatively, Badrfam and colleagues analyzed data about suicidal thoughts and burnout and their association among healthcare workers in Iran after the fourth wave of the pandemic (72).The paper published by Msetfi et al. analyzed pandemic-collected data and 1) assessed the correlation between feelings of control and depression, 2) explored if varying control measures influenced this correlation, and 3) determined if this relationship was altered based on pandemic indicators (73).Finally, we included six papers that presented data, reflections, or proposals for the management of the future or long-term COVID-19 consequences. Nisa and colleagues hypothesized that the COVID-19 pandemic could represent a pivotal moment in global backing for universal health coverage, as indicated by a heightened agreement regarding the government's roles as a healthcare provider (74). Ransing and a team of early-career psychiatrists from different countries discussed, in a positive and optimistic vision, the substantial international scientific collaboration during and after the pandemic, as demonstrated by the increase in multidisciplinary and international scientific literature (75). Wagner et al. emphasized the necessity of enhancing communication and accessibility to mental health services in higher education. Recommendations and implications for policy and support services were outlined (76). Mejia and his team conducted a cross-sectional survey examining the prevalence of risk for post-traumatic stress disorder following COVID-19 across 12 countries in Latin America (77) Finally, in Columbia, Bautista-Gomez et al. examined the country's specific psychosocial risk profiles to manage future health emergencies (79).As of May 2024, the World Health Organization reported more than 775 million confirmed cases of COVID-19 worldwide, and over 7 million deaths directly related to the coronavirus, as well as incalculable damage to physical health, mental health, and quality of life around the world (80)(81)(82). At the same time, through the efforts of frontliners, physicians, and researchers, the articles collected in this eighth and previous seven volumes, demonstrate a beacon of hope towards better understanding and facing the challenge of the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on mental health, allowing to draw robust conclusions and expectations for the years to come (83)(84)(85).

title: Economic crisis situation facing Iraq; an effect of Corona virus pandemic. (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND If we study historical data on GDP growth from a large panel of countries, we observe that historically, sharp increases in search activity, in particular for the “recession topic’’, are associated with subsequently sharp contractions in growth rates – in particular, consumption growth. We find that a 100% increase in search intensity for the “recession topic’’ in a quarter vis-à-vis the country-specific average intensity is associated with a 1.5 percentage points lower growth in consumption or a 1 percentage point lower growth in real GDP in the subsequent quarter. What may lie behind these economic anxieties? And how can the economic fallout be limited? To shed some light on this, we conduct an online survey experiment in a nationally representative sample with around 1000 participants from the US on March 4th. Through an online survey experiment conducted in partnership with Luc.id in a representative sample of the US population, we shed light on the underlying mechanisms through which the new coronavirus may be driving economic anxieties. We elicit peoples’ beliefs about both the case mortality and its contagiousness (R0) and contrast this with what the medical literature has documented so far. The WHO recently estimated that the mortality of Covid19 disease triggered by the new coronavirus is around 3.4%. Earlier estimates were closer to 2%. The contagiousness R0 was estimated around 2. Empirically, the beliefs about mortality are quite heterogeneous. More than 50% of respondents think mortality is higher than 5% (average at 19%). This seems substantially higher than what the medical literature on the new coronavirus suggests to date. The beliefs about contagiousness are also heterogeneous, with 50% of respondents thinking that every infected person infects at least 10 others. The average is substantially higher with 43. Refineries are cutting production of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Pipeline operators are telling producers that they can ship crude only if there is a buyer willing to take the fuel because storage tanks are filling up fast. Oil companies are dropping rigs, dismissing frocking crews and beginning to shut down wells. As much as 20 percent or 20 million barrels a day, of oil demand may be lost as the global economy slows, according to the International Energy Agency. . (Cliford claus march 31 2020 newyork times)That is roughly equivalent to eliminating all U.S. consumption. To make matters worse, Saudi Arabia and Russia are increasing oil production to regain market share from American oil companies that increased production and exports in recent years. Global oil benchmark prices hover around $20 a barrel — levels not seen in a generation — and regional prices in West Texas and North Dakota have fallen even further, to around $10 a barrel. Besides, Iraq has a renter and consumption budget rather than a developmental one. All revenues from oil and other resources feed salaries.” She added, “The dwindling revenues lead to dropping salaries and this is a new disaster for Iraqis, in addition to the deficit reaching $51 billion. title: President's Address. The Transplantation Society—Vancouver 2010
abstract: It is a time for reflection as we turn the page of this decade and face a new one. In my presidential address, I want to examine the challenges that lie ahead of us primarily as a consequence of the success that the last decade of progress has created in the field of transplantation. If we could look into the eyes of our forebears, such as Alexis Carrel, Rene Kuss, Sir Peter Medawar, MacFarlane Burnet, David Hume, and Joseph Murray, and ask them whether we have accomplished what they imagined could be done and what they worked to achieve, what would they reply? We are still able to ask some of those who have set the stage for success and whose work defined our ability to achieve today's results—Is this what you hoped for? Being the people that they are, pleased as they may be by the results achieved today, their sights are still set higher on our holy grail of allograft tolerance. The number and complexity of transplants that are performed across the world are increasing steadily, including kidney, liver and heart, pancreas, lung, intestine, and islet transplants. We must not forget the remarkable success of the face and hand transplants, the cornea, and the devascularized structural transplants—heart valves, bones, bone paste, teeth, and skin. We must also recall the fields of bone marrow, peripheral blood stem cells, cord blood stem cells, and the more experimental cellular transplants of mesenchymal origin. We are in a position to match two individuals at 10 human leukocyte antigen loci and undertake a bone marrow transplant for an individual in one country derived from the altruism of an individual from another, because of a global network with more than 14 million tissue-typed individuals. Transplantation of the kidney is the therapy of choice—the patients' choice, the medical choice, and the governmental choice. Economics and outcomes are joined together in a happy alignment. Thus, even countries with middle Human Development Index economies are striving to increase kidney transplantation rates as an alternative to the much too expensive therapy of maintenance dialysis. There is, however, a substantial spread of transplantation rates even in the high Human Development Index countries, with Spain, Austria, Norway, and the United States at the top; Australia and Canada languishing in the middle; and Japan with all the work ahead of them—starting successfully this year because of changes to their laws in 2009. The results that we saw twinkling in the eyes of the pioneers are perhaps here today for a number of organ types and from a number of countries or regions. It is not uncommon for 1-year functional survival of deceased and living donor kidney transplants to be in the mid-90%, although the results are not as good when the recipient has been transplanted previously. There is still progress to be made to improve the early results of heart, lung, and liver transplants, but we are well on the way to formidable success there too. In the longer term, we are failing to achieve the results we would like, with liver transplantation for nonmalignant disease and bone marrow transplantation giving us the most long-term stability. The 40-year kidney transplant graft survival results should give us all a cause for thought before we celebrate the successes too openly or too prematurely, just as the mortality rates give us a dose of reality comparing the normal population with the dialysis and transplant populations. We have a log order of improvement required before we can say that we have cured the disease and its consequences for the individual. So, the consequence of short-term success with transplantation is to drive waiting lists for most organ transplants to unachievable levels. Despite many negative influences on patients entering the waiting list, “lottery of life” as it has been portrayed, the waiting times and numbers increase inexorably everywhere. In Australia, we have 7-year waiting times, and only a small proportion of the dialysis population is actually active on the list. Around the world, there are few countries that can boast of stable waiting list numbers, let alone claim to be making inroads into waiting times. Donation is clearly the most important limiting factor. It is not the only limitation of course, with trained medical and nursing workforces, and laboratory and hospital infrastructure also relevant factors in some countries. The demand that we have created by our actual and even more so by our purported success and our failure to respond by increasing transplantation rates has ensured that our patients are caught in a maelstrom of decisions and are ready to fall victim to the internet brokers and the illusionary tales of easy outcomes in clean, well-staffed clinics in other lands. Perhaps, 10% of the 100,000 transplants performed each year in the period from 2005 to 2008 were the results of human trafficking and transplant tourism. Estimates of 3500 liver transplants in China in 2006 suggest that an estimate of 1800 executions that year was a significant underestimate. Pakistan as one epicenter of the trade in living donor suffering was processing 2 to 3000 kidneys from the indentured farm laborers. In the Philippines, the trade was just as brisk from the slums and the waste tips of Manilla and Quezon City, encouraged and fermented by the brokers. Do we stand by and decry this trade, or do we join forces and work with the international and national jurisdictions to do something to highlight and to stop this? Are we not as the professionals in the field who have taught the techniques and have developed the drugs and the laboratory tests fully responsible for the way in which our knowledge is used? We are not the scientists of the Manhattan Project, but I contend that we do carry a responsibility. The Transplantation Society has traveled the world in the past few years and interacted at all levels with many governments. The membership off our society, working in each country, has tackled both the sources of the donors and the sources of the transplant tourists. Those working in the rich economies have sought to stop patients from wanting to travel, whereas those working in the poor economies have needed to seek protection of their vulnerable populations. In Israel and Saudi Arabia, for example, different actions have resulted in dramatic decreases in transplant tourists. The former driven by prevention of insurance company payments for therapy that would be illegal in Israel and the latter by finding solutions to the organ donor shortages at home and providing the resources to undertake the transplants. In China, the law is now clear, and we applaud that legal regulation of abuses, the like of which we have seen nowhere else. But there is now such extensive evidence of the flouting of the laws that one has to wonder whether a country as well organized and capable as China economically and militarily cannot exert its will in the simple matter of a number of hospitals selling organs to foreigners. Bringing to court a couple of people involved in murder for organs is not enough when patients continue to flow into the country on a daily basis from our renal and liver programs across the world. In Pakistan, Adib Rizvi has conducted a 20-year campaign to stop the trade in Lahore and Rawalpindi. The World Health Organization (WHO) and The Transplantation Society (TTS) have been there to support him and congratulate him on achieving change in the law with unanimous upper and lower house passage of the Human Organ Transplant Act to stop this trade. Our applause for this work is well deserved by our colleagues in Pakistan, but it would be naive to assume that the simple passage of a law—just as in China—will change the lucrative habits of the hospitals and the brokers. Sale of an organ is now illegal in both countries, and our task becomes one of holding governments accountable for implementing their own laws. In May 2008, your society, in conjunction with the International Society of Nephrology, brought 150 people with a variety of different backgrounds, from 78 countries, to Istanbul to debate definitions and consider professional standards of practice to protect the rights of the human organ donor. The Declaration of Istanbul has been endorsed by approximately 100 organizations—that is, by national nephrology and transplant societies, by some national governmental organizations, and by some in the pharmaceutical industry. Journals are starting to enquire whether clinical studies conform to these principles, and national ethics review committees meeting in Singapore recently examined the role that the Declaration may play in their approval processes. The Declaration of Istanbul Custodian Group will keep the declaration alive, just as the World Medical Association has kept the Declaration of Helsinki a live document for more than 50 years, to ensure that we have widely accepted professional standards for the protection of the rights of the human organ donor. In May 2010, the member states of the World Health Assembly unanimously passed a resolution endorsing the revised WHO Guiding Principles for human organ transplantation. The resolution confirms that the nations of the world will not tolerate payment for organs and are intent on improved regulation of the field. It was a 7-year journey to achieve this resolution, and it was disturbing only a few weeks later to find a health minister espouse “rewarded gifting”—a minister from a country in which some of the worst abuses of the poor have been documented. Is this the untrammeled power of money or of the ends justifying the means? Is this just another euphemism on the road to abuse of the poor and vulnerable? The message for us as professionals in the field of transplantation is that the dominating power of the rich over the poor and the success of transplantation as a therapy will forever leave us practicing with global tension between the rich and the poor. It is important that we now work to provide answers to the problems that our success has created. TTS, the Organización Nacional de Transplantes, and the WHO moved on from the World Health Assembly Resolution, even before it was passed. It is now essential to provide the framework for national governments to do something meaningful to reduce the toll of death that accompanies the now treatable chronic organ failures. Clearly, not all nations of the world are economically capable of assuming responsibility for all diseases nor of providing all answers. But all nations of the world must make decisions about what they can and what they cannot afford to do. A guidance document will soon be appearing as a result of a meeting held in Madrid under the aegis of the WHO and in conjunction with TTS and the Organización Nacional de Transplantes. This conceptual overview of disease management from prevention and education through to the high technologies of transplantation will help us all to argue for the resources needed in each of our environments. Just as we have created the knowledge base for successful transplantation and have assembled the skills that are needed around the world to provide this therapy, we must drive the knowledge needed to provide the organs that our therapy demands. The solutions will most likely come from countries successfully retrieving large numbers of deceased donor organs and from countries where the largest numbers of living donors are providing kidneys for their relatives. It may also come partly from development of technology to resuscitate organs not transplantable today because of ischemic damage. We will undoubtedly have to expend at least as much, if not more, energy on these issues, as our forebears have spent making a routinely available treatment from one perceived to be dangerous, unsuccessful, and unaffordable by most nations. We have other scientific challenges created by our successes. These must be thought about carefully if we are not to fall by the wayside as our compatriots on the technology trail—such as oncology, hematology, neurology, virology, and bacteriology—drive solutions to those diseases through technological innovation. The success that we have achieved to date is changing the decisions made in research environments about where to invest. The results in kidney transplant control groups at 1 and even 2 years are so good now that pharmaceutical companies are hesitant to invest in the clinical studies required for drug development. Earlier this year, TTS brought together scientists involved in technology development—the 100-channel flow cytometer, the groups with the goal of a handheld, battery-powered genome sequencer and the makers of tiny lanterns to light the way to the cells' interior—with scientists involved in applying those new technologies to clinical transplantation. Minnie Sarwal named it Transplantomics, and the name has stuck. This was a meeting for clinical transplant leaders, for technology developers, and also for the regulators and industry. Transplantomics will be an annual meeting because we will need continuous progress in science to provide some of the answers that we need if we are to provide better therapy in the future. The Transplantation Society has approximately 5000 members worldwide, we have close affiliations with 11 national transplant societies, there are seven special interest sections, and we have increasingly close relationships with all the major regional transplant societies. TTS remains an NGO in official relations with the WHO, and we are in constant communication with governments across the world. We have provided scholarships for approximately 100 people to attend the XXIII Congress of The Transplantation Society in Vancouver—some are young investigators on whom we place the burdens of the future, and others are from emerging economies striving to carry their burdens today. We wish them the challenges of the successes that transplantation represents today. Thank you for the honor to serve as your president for these past 2 years.

title: Life in the Time of COVID-19
abstract: COVID-19: COVID-19The COVID-19 (Coronavirus Disease-2019) world pandemic is still in the mid-phases in most of the world. It may persist for several months, or even longer. In some geographies that ignored its early threat (Spain, Italy), COVID-19 spread rapidly and overwhelmed medical infrastructures: hospital beds, ICU beds, respirators, dialysis machines, personal protective equipment (PPE), and health care workers. This extended to areas with COVID-19 spread-enhancing features: cosmopolitan, high influx of tourism, dense populations, mass transit, poorer neighborhoods with close quarters and multigenerational families, large events (Mardi Gras in New Orleans; soccer game with 40,000 attendance in Lombardy, Italy). In these epicenters, COVID-19 has been associated with higher mortality rates (10-12% in Spain and Italy), and high infection rates among health care workers (10-20%). COVID-19 continues to infect millions and cause the deaths of tens of thousands. These figures may be underestimations because of lack of widespread testing, autopsies, and reporting. The virus is weakening world economies and large and small industries, particularly in the sectors of oil, services, tourism, transportation, sports, and the arts. It is also rapidly changing our social habits and norms into what might become a “new normal” life. As of April 17, 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic had infected 2.2+ million people worldwide and caused the death of 147,000+. In the United States, 672,000+ people had been infected, with 33,000 deaths. In the early phases of the pandemic, the prevalence of the infection (total number of infected people) increased by 33% daily, which means it doubled every 3 days.1 By mid-April, the doubling rate had increased to 7 days, confirming the benefits of COVID-19 preventive measures: enhanced hygiene, PPE, social distancing; geographic lock-downs; and COVID-19 testing, contact tracing, and isolation. This also suggests that, rather than causing widespread and overwhelming COVID-19 surges, the disease may simmer in a “slow-motion” waxing and waning status until we develop safe and effective anti-COVID-19 vaccines and treatments. This is unless we are happily surprised by one of the following: 1) the virus gradually undergoes mutations that make it less infective (as with influenza); 2) the viral spread is suppressed by warmer, humid weather (seasonal spread); or 3) “herd immunity” develops faster than expected (as measured by blood testing for COVID-19 neutralizing antibodies). This will be discussed later. Still important but as yet unknown parameters that influence the final toll of COVID-19 are: 1) Will it recur in waves? 2) Will it then become more or less virulent? 3) Will COVID-19 IgG neutralizing antibodies provide durable immunity? Recent estimates from other coronaviruses suggest protection for months to 2 years. And 4) how quickly will safe and effective vaccines and treatments become available? On a personal note, one of the authors (H.K.) had discussions with medical oncology colleagues in several countries in the Middle East (Lebanon, Jordan, Israel, Saudi Arabia, and Iran). It is their impression that COVID-19, with social restrictions but minimal testing, is less common and less fatal in this part of the world. This simply may be due to insufficient testing or reporting, but there is also the possibility that COVID-19 is not thriving in these geographies (warmer, humid weather), or that it has mutated to a less virulent form. Time will tell. The Spread of COVID-19 The first cases of COVID-19 were found in China in mid-November 2019, but not reported until later. The disease abated there in early March, after severe social restrictions and wide COVID-19 screening, isolation, and prevention.2 Some experts criticized China for its early delays and lack of transparency/data sharing, and are questioning its reported cases, particularly the number of deaths, which may be higher. Some countries had experience with previous regional epidemics like severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS).3 They took the threat seriously, developing early COVID testing and wide screening, contact tracing and isolation, and social distancing. They were able to contain the COVID-19 spread earlier and more effectively. These include South Korea, Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, and Taiwan. However, COVID-19 started spreading again once protective measures were eased. Countries that had no prior experiences with viral epidemics, and that delayed testing and protective measures, experienced significantly higher infection and mortality rates (Spain, Italy, France, and England). The United States did not appreciate the potential COVID-19 threat early on, had significant delays (about 6-8 weeks) in wide testing due to development and manufacturing issues,4 and delayed implementing social distancing and restrictions. We are still mid-pandemic, and testing and protective measures will definitely reduce the final toll of COVID-19, as has been observed in the past week in several cities and regions. What Can We Learn From Previous Viral Epidemics? COVID-19 is not “like influenza,” as has been suggested. The influenza season of 2017-2018 infected 45 million Americans and caused the death of 61,000, a mortality rate of about 0.13%.5 The estimated mortality rate from COVID-19 is so far about 5%, 30-40 times higher than that of influenza. The difference in mortality rates in different geographies may relate to several factors: extent of testing; protection measures; effect of warmer, humid weather (still in question); medical infrastructure capacities; number and prevalence of preexisting conditions; viral genetic variations; reporting; and others. For example, about 25-50% of COVID-19 infected patients may be asymptomatic. Therefore, wide COVID-19 testing increases the incidence of reported COVID-19 clinical infections. This results in a lower reported mortality rate. Limited screening (e.g., by the Centers for Disease Control & Prevention criteria) would only capture more symptomatic and severe cases, producing a higher reported mortality rate. In addition, the mortality rate may be significantly higher among patients with cancer due to their immunocompromised state. Small cohort studies suggest one as high as 30+%.6 The “Spanish influenza” pandemic of 1918-1920 was the most devastating on record. It recurred in 3 waves, the second being the most virulent, infected a third of the world population (500 million of 1.5 billion), and resulted in an estimated 50 million deaths (mortality rate 10% over the 3 waves).7 However, there were no vaccines or drugs then to mitigate the spread of the virus, no antibiotics to treat secondary infections, little understanding of the pathophysiology of diseases, and nothing to compare with the incredible research resources and medical infrastructures that exist today. The swine flu of 2009 infected 60 million Americans and caused the death of about 12,500 (mortality rate 0.02%). A safe and effective vaccine available then mitigated the viral spread and reduced mortality.9 COVID-19 is highly contagious, airborne, and survives on inert surfaces for a few hours to several days, depending on the ambient temperatures and conditions.10-13 Seasonal influenza transmits from 1 person to 1.2 others; COVID-19 transmits from 1 person to 6-7 without precautions, and to 2-3 with precautions. It is important to note that infectivity actually may be highest before the onset of symptoms. This explains why COVID-19 is difficult to control without wide testing by nasal swabs and blood serology for COVID-19 neutralizing IgG (discussed below), and if social protective measures are relaxed before herd immunity develops from viral exposure or vaccines.11,12 The long-term health care impact of the COVID-19 pandemic will probably be significantly less severe than that of the 1918-1920 Spanish influenza. The health care and economic effects of the 1918-20 Spanish influenza were closely intertwined with the post-World War 1 consequences (infrastructure destruction, poor nutrition, poor medical support, vast migrations). In contrast, only 4 months into the COVID-19 pandemic, millions of researchers and most large health care companies and public health care infrastructures worldwide are investing huge amounts of time and resources, and billions of dollars to investigate hundreds of potential vaccines and treatments. Even as of mid-April, many hopeful leads are coming through. Also the benefits of wide testing and protective social measures are already showing positive trends for COVID-19 suppression in many geographies. Herd Immunity & Importance of Wide Testing From historical data, we know that viral spread can be controlled once a proportion of a population becomes immune, through either exposure to the virus or vaccination. This percent depends on the infectivity of a particular virus and availability of an effective vaccine. For COVID-19, it is estimated that 60% of a particular population needs to be exposed and/or vaccinated. With regard to testing, a distinction should be made between COVID-19 “exposure,” measured by blood IgG serology, and “clinical infection,” measured by nasal swabs, since up to 50% of exposed people may never exhibit symptoms. From the existing data (with very limited testing by nasal swabs and even less serologic testing), it is estimated that less that 1-2% of the world population has been clinically infected. To get a precise estimate of “exposure” and how long herd immunity will take to develop, we need wide serology testing to detect the virus-specific IgG antibody. This is not just a simple epidemiologic exercise. It will help identify different “COVID-19 immunologic profiles,” protect lives, reduce mortality, and revive economies faster (discussed later). Ending the COVID-19 pandemic and seeing light at the end of the COVID-19 tunnel will happen if any of these conditions are met: 1) Herd immunity through exposure to COVID-19 that covers 60% of people.14 2) Development of effective and safe vaccines. Short of a vaccine, the development of effective anti-COVID-19 treatments, as with AIDS, where a vaccine could not be developed, but highly effective drugs exist. 3) Any of the following happy “black swans” occur—COVID-19 virus develops mutations that weaken and eliminate it (as happens with influenza); it is suppressed by warmer humid weathers (seasonal, giving enough time to develop vaccines); serology testing shows exposure and herd immunity developing much faster than expected; or exposure results in many years (rather than months) of immunity. COVID-19 Testing Nasal swab testing (PCR testing) identifies people with an active SARS-CoV-2 infection, the virus that causes COVID-19. This test gives results in 5 minutes, using small portable devices that can be deployed widely in all health care facilities. COVID-19 testing in the blood (serology test) involves measuring the immune response of the body to the viral exposure. An early non-specific IgM immune response develops about 5 days after exposure. A second more selective COVID-19 neutralizing IgG antibody immune response develops 2-4 weeks later. Based on the COVID-19 testing, individuals may fall into different “COVID-19 immunity profile” groups. The first are those who are COVID-19 negative by both nasal and serologic tests. These are still at risk. The second are those with positive PCR nasal swabs. These are infected and can infect others, and they must be isolated to avoid the viral spread. The third are those who have recovered from a COVID-19 infection and have developed COVID-19 IgG antibodies (positive serology). These individuals are probably resistant to a reinfection. They protect others as buffers in crowds. They may be able to donate plasma (rich with anti-COVID–specific IgG) to treat severely ill patients. They can also return safely to work and, if they are health care workers, they can be deployed preferentially to treat infected patients. Defining different COVID-19 risk groups can be used to prevent the COVID-19 spread, protect and treat patients, reinvigorate industries and work places, and reopen and normalize societal venues. However, there may be unintended consequences. For example, poorer and out-of-work Americans without income or resources may potentially take a risk and purposefully infect themselves to become immune and be able to work again. During high-risk COVID-19 periods, capacities should be scaled to enable testing any individual with any symptoms, and to conduct COVID-19 serology testing on all individuals at the start, then periodically (every month). COVID-19 testing may become routine, like measuring the blood pressure, the temperature, or blood sugar and chemistry levels. At least a million nasal swabs and blood serologies may need to be done daily, and be easily available across all health care facilities. As happened in some nursing homes, health care facilities may be easy venues for COVID-19 spread (mini-epicenters), because of the presence of dense populations of vulnerable patients, and frequent contacts with health care workers. Testing and social protective measures in medical facilities should be even more intense. Summary Life in the time of COVID-19 will certainly be different from the past. In high-risk COVID-19 periods, testing should be widespread, as discussed. In addition, the new normal in our lives will include: 1) Better hygiene and social distancing. This will not only prevent COVID-19, but may also reduce mortality for other viral infections, such as influenza. 2) Fewer physical gatherings, more virtual communications, and enhanced telecommuting capabilities. 3) Universal health care and better-prepared health care facilities. This will provide equal and optimal access to medical care for all Americans in such stressful times, without fears of lack of insurance, catastrophic medical bills, rejection of care, etc. 4) Elimination of unnecessary bureaucracies that have accumulated over decades across multiple disciplines, for example in health care and medical research. These bureaucracies have not improved quality of care, research, or patient safety. They have, however, slowed progress, added multiple layers of administrative burdens, and increased costs 3- to 10-fold. Some of the above measures have already demonstrated favorable trends towards reducing global warming. Finally, enhanced capacity for preparedness is essential to be able to effectively face new viral pandemics and other potential catastrophes. HAGOP KANTARJIAN, MD, is a medical oncologist and a Special Fellow of Health Policies at the Baker Institute, Rice University. MARY ALMA WELCH, MMSC, is a physician assistant in Houston. STEVEN KORNBLAU, MD, is a medical oncologist in Houston. ANDREW DINARDO, MD, is an infectious disease specialist in Houston. NADIM AJAMI, PHD, is a virologist and microbiologist who specializes in virome and microbiome research. title: Social Scientific Perspectives on the Rescue Flights Scandal
abstract: The scandal involving the “rescue flights” in Vietnam broke in early 2023, three years after COVID-19 had spread across the world and created a global crisis. The scandal involved fifty-four officials in five central ministries and several cities and provinces, including a deputy minister, several ambassadors, deputy mayors, and advisors to the deputy prime minister and other ministers. The officials were charged with receiving millions of dollars in bribes for discharging their official duties, which were to review and approve flights to bring home (“rescue”) Vietnamese citizens stranded abroad because of COVID-19. Many private business owners who had offered the bribes were also brought to trial. During the investigation, some of them had bribed senior police officers, and those officers (a major general and a lieutenant colonel) ended up being arrested and put on trial as well.This bribery case has been called one of the “largest and most complex corruption cases ever in [Vietnamese] history” and a “national disgrace” [nỗi đau của đất nước].1 It eventually led to the resignation of First Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Bình Minh, who had been a candidate for higher positions but whose secretary was one of those put on trial. This essay examines the scandal from various social scientific perspectives, from political economy to sociocultural analysis and historical sociology. Each of these perspectives offers useful concepts to explain the scandal and sheds light on different aspects of the event. The purpose of this exercise is not to decide which theoretical perspective has greater explanatory power but to provide a range of lenses through which Vietnam’s opaque politics can be understood.For more than a year after the pandemic emerged, Vietnam implemented a zero-Covid policy, which involved closing off the border, aggressively monitoring the disease, and imposing strict quarantines of entire neighborhoods when cases were detected. As a result of border closures, tens of thousands of Vietnamese citizens, of whom migrant workers were perhaps the largest group, needed or desired to return to Vietnam but could not do so. The first “rescue flight” took place on February 10, 2020, to bring home thirty Vietnamese citizens who were stranded in locked-down Wuhan, China. The official purpose of this flight, which left Vietnam on February 2, 2020, was actually to bring Vietnamese donations of medical aid to Wuhan as a friendly gesture to China, but the Vietnamese government allowed its stranded citizens there to piggyback on the return trip, apparently for free. Following this flight, President Nguyễn Xuân Phúc ordered government agencies to arrange for Vietnamese citizens who needed or wanted to return home under Vietnam’s policy of “protection of citizens [abroad]” [bảo hộ công dân].2 The five ministries tasked with this mission included Foreign Affairs, Health, Public Security, Defense, and Transportation. Representatives of the participating ministries formed a committee that was presided over by Tô Anh Dũng, a deputy minister of Foreign Affairs. Flights specifically for “rescue” purposes were authorized to meet the demand among Vietnamese working, studying, living, or simply stranded abroad. Many were drawn home by the relatively calm situation in Vietnam compared to many other countries, such as Spain, South Korea, and the United States, where the pandemic was spreading rapidly, overwhelming medical facilities, and causing thousands of deaths.By mid-2021, about one thousand such flights (or about two flights per day on average) had taken place, bringing about two hundred thousand people back to Vietnam.3 At around the same time, fearing an economic downturn due to the loss of tourists, the Vietnamese government partially lifted the ban on commercial flights into and out of the country. The government also greenlighted private companies to operate flights to bring home those Vietnamese nationals abroad who wanted to return and could afford to pay the cost. These flights, called “combo” by the Vietnamese authorities, would still need the approval of the five-ministry committee. Approved private companies were to solicit customers or receive the names of those who registered with Vietnamese embassies abroad, collect payment, rent aircrafts and flight crews, and arrange with airport and provincial authorities for airport transfers and quarantine facilities in Vietnam to accommodate returnees for two weeks upon arrival. It appears that selection for these flights was based solely on ability to pay for expenses rather than on an assessment of a given individual’s need to return home.According to documents provided to the court and reported in the media, hundreds of private companies submitted bids for contracts to provide repatriation services. These included some legitimate tour companies and some apparently without any expertise in international transport or tourism. Information provided by the Ministry of Public Security showed that more than one hundred companies were approved, but only twenty carried out operations.4 Yet according to the executives who testified in court, the process dragged out, and the companies were kept waiting for approval, held up by various obstacles. To secure timely approval, these companies sought an audience with members of the government committee through personal connections and offered bribes to the officials in the committee or in Vietnamese embassies abroad. During their testimonies in court, officials explained that they had viewed these bribes as personal “gifts” to indicate appreciation for their kindness. In contrast, business executives testifying at the trial saw the gifts as fees that must be paid to facilitate a business transaction. They revealed that some officials, such as Phạm Trung Kiên, the secretary of Deputy Minister of Health Đỗ Xuân Tuyên, actually yelled at them [quát mắng] and directly demanded money up front in return for approval.These contrasting interpretations of the payments aside, there is no doubt that large sums of cash did change hands, reportedly a total of 9.3 million US dollars or 226 billion đồng. These transactions occurred at coffee shops, inside cars, and at the private homes of officials; some took place directly, others through intermediaries. Nearly two thousand flights had taken place by the end of 2022 when the investigation started, and passengers often paid at least twice the normal round-trip price for a one-way ticket. According to a housemaid who worked in Saudi Arabia, the airfare for one such flight from Riyadh to Vietnam cost between 1,300 and 2,600 US dollars (28–62 million đồng), exclusive of charges related to quarantine once arriving in Vietnam.5In the remainer of this essay I will apply relevant social scientific concepts to analyze the scandal and its implications for Vietnamese politics. First, from a political economy perspective, the criminal practices in this case could simply be described in terms of price gouging and government–business collusion under conditions of monopolistic supply. Only those companies that offered bribes were allowed to operate repatriation flights, and they could dictate high prices, part of which would go to pay for the bribes. The scandal could have been avoided if the government had called for public bids by private businesses to provide air transportation to customers at costs that, though expensive, would at least be competitive. For deserving folks who could not afford to pay, the government would pick up the tab—again, in a transparent manner. The scandal was made possible because officials did not want to use a bidding process. Given that Vietnamese consulates and embassies abroad commonly practice price gouging when it comes to visas,6 they must have seen an opportunity to profit from the situation. At the same time, top government leaders (ministers and higher) chose not to intervene to protect their fellow citizens from the profiteers.The explanation above focuses on the mismatch between demand and supply caused by COVID-19, the closure of borders, and the lack of a competitive business environment in Vietnam. Yet it is well known that in its “market economy with socialist orientation,” the Vietnamese government still intervenes deeply in the market.7 Officials as owners of public resources routinely collect lucrative amounts of “rent” from state-owned enterprises and private businesses in return for access to such resources.8 While the business environment is not competitive, rivalries among politicians’ personal patronage networks can be intense, which explains why scandals like this one sometimes get exposed.In contrast with the political economy approach, a sociocultural perspective analyzes the scandal in the light of Vietnam’s socialist past. In this perspective, the scandal can be explained as a natural, if particularly egregious, outcome of the well-known “envelope culture” [văn hoá phong bì] and xin-cho [begging and granting] practices [thói quen xin-cho] embedded in the social structure of communist Vietnam and prevalent in the administrative practices of the Vietnamese government. Envelope culture and xin-cho practices, especially the latter, in turn, are traceable to the decades when the Vietnamese Communist Party sought to implement a socialist system. In that system (called bao cấp, or subsidy), the government deeply penetrated into individuals’ lives and assumed responsibility for the provision of most basic consumer goods and social services, from healthcare to education. Most citizens were employed by the government, as members of either rural cooperatives or state-owned enterprises. No private entities were permitted to provide goods and services, which were a government monopoly. Yet while keeping its monopoly on consumer goods and service provision, the party prioritized wars and (in times of peace) socialist industrialization. It demanded that the population sacrifice for socialism, rather than looking after their daily needs. With extremely limited resources devoted to public services and consumer goods, only the highest-ranking officials and their families received adequate services as rewards for their positions. For the rest of the population, services and goods were of very poor quality in all respects, and one had to beg [xin] to be granted [cho]. Petty corruption was widespread, as government officials could demand “gifts” (normally goods or cash, but also in other forms) for any services or goods to be obtained, especially services or goods of higher-than-normal quality.In the deeply hierarchial socialist society in Vietnam, the party-state could be likened to a ruthless boss; state officials occupied the top rung of the system, hoarding all its power and privileges. While the Vietnamese system today is socialist only in name, the “rescue flights” scandal suggests that the party-state remains ruthless, and officials still dominate the political, economic, and social hierarchy. Although envelope culture may be viewed as part of traditional gift-giving practices in Vietnamese culture, the contending claims between officials and business executives in the scandal suggest that asymmetric power relationships and the ruthless culture of officialdom, rather than benign customs, were at the roots of the behavior. Remarkably, the government did not acknowledge these relationships, preferring to blame such behavior on the poor morality or degeneracy of officials [tha hoá, thoái hoá, or tự chuyển hoá].While the sociocultural perspective evokes Vietnam’s recent socialist past, the view from historical sociology calls attention to its path to state formation through war and revolution. In Charles Tilly’s formulation of “the state as organized crime,” a mafia rather than a ruthless boss would serve as a more apt image for the party-state.9 Tilly studies state formation in late medieval and early modern Western Europe, an extremely violent process during which modern states emerged out of the struggle for power, territory, and population among monarchs, feudal lords, merchants, and religious leaders. In return for protection, rulers demanded labor and rents from their population, which is very similar to the relationship between street gangs and people who live on their turf. As Tilly argues, “if protection rackets represent organized crime at its smoothest, then war making and state making—quintessential protection rackets with the advantage of legitimacy—qualify as our largest examples of organized crime. Without branding all generals and statesmen as murderers or thieves, I want to urge the value of that analogy.”10Tilly’s analogy supplies a particularly useful heuristic for the rescue flights scandal, in which Vietnamese officials and their business cronies relied on the party-state as a tool to extort money from citizens—ostensibly in exchange for protection from the pandemic. The analogy is also apt in explaining the Việt-Á test kit scandal that broke at the same time. In that case, citizens were forced to pay a high price for mediocre and, in some cases, useless products that were supposed to protect them from the virus. The scheme was deployed and enforced by the government under its zero-Covid policy, which mandated frequent testing for workers in industrial zones, patients and visitors at hospitals, and people in other contexts at their own expense. However, the analogy does not work well for other kinds of corruption scandals in which officials embezzled money from the government, such as the recent scandal involving the Xuyên Việt Tour and Oil Transport Company, which imports and retails petroleum, or the corruption case involving the Vietnamese Navy’s Command of Coastal Patrol [Bộ Tư Lệnh Cảnh Sát Biển].11 These cases did not involve large populations or an exchange of security protection for payment.The idea of the state as a mafia that extorts citizens in exchange for (imagined or real) protection is still not as appalling as the “predatory state,” the archetypical form of the “developmental state” in sociologist Peter Evans’s framework, which examines the different roles of states in economic development.12 Predatory states ruthlessly extract and plunder resources from society without concern for the welfare of citizens or long-term economic development. In contrast, “developmental states” are able to nurture economic transformation even though they also siphon off some resources for their own benefit. The officials charged in the rescue flights scandal clearly behaved in a predatory manner: They took advantage of the situation to profit, without any concern for their victims—among whom were such vulnerable compatriots as housemaids in Saudi Arabia and those recently released from Malaysian prisons.Officials’ predatory behavior in the rescue flights is systematic and institutionalized in the Vietnamese state, as observed by two researchers-cum-long-term policy consultants to the government:At present, off-budget operations and illicit activities are commonplace in all state organizations at all levels.…Informal practices go far beyond ordinary modes of bureaucratic corruption. They are much more strategic, systemic, and highly institutionalized in an informally commercialized administrative culture. Examples include running private firms under the names of relatives and straw men to feed them with public contracts, trading state positions for cash and favors, auctioning off licenses, informally renting out public property, grabbing land in the context of fuzzy property regimes, collecting informal levies, capitalizing on insider information on land speculations, bid-rigging in public procurement, nurturing private firms in the shadow of state enterprise, and siphoning off large profits in state monopolies.…Whether bureaucrats are individually or collectively organized, the ingenuity by which they capitalize on their public offices and privileged access to state resources knows little limit.13According to this account, most incumbent officials are out for themselves, not for the public interest, even while they ostensibly serve the public. Unlike former Zaire, which is the country Evans uses as an exemplar of a predatory state, Vietnam has seen economic growth, albeit not at a transformative level (i.e., a level that would have turned Vietnam into an industrialized country, like South Korea or Taiwan, after three decades).
