title: The Routledge Handbook of CoFuturisms
abstract: Futuristic imaginaries have long been disputed on account of hegemonic Western perspectives and the legacies of colonial complicity of speculative genres such as science fiction and fantasy. A more complex history of these genres and the continuous diversification of futurisms that writers, artists, and scholars of color have demanded for decades, has been achieved not least due to a range of anthologies and magazines, often including programmatic statements or manifestos. Some key interventions in the field include Dark Matter: A Century of Speculative Fiction from the African Diaspora, edited by Sheree R. Thomas (2000); So Long Been Dreaming: Postcolonial Science Fiction and Fantasy, edited by Nalo Hopkinson and Uppinder Mehan (2004); Walking the Clouds: An Anthology of Indigenous Science Fiction, edited by Grace L. Dillon (2012); and We See a Different Frontier: A Postcolonial Speculative Fiction Anthology, edited by Djibri al-Ayad and Fabio Fernandes (2013). Afrofuturism, from its coinage by Mark Dery in conversation with Black artists and critics in 1993 to Ytasha L. Womack’s Afrofuturism: The World of Black Sci-Fi and Fantasy Culture (2013) and many other studies in between and since then, has been productively complicated by Nnedi Okorafor’s widely circulated conceptualization of Africanfuturism as an Africa-centered complementary notion in “Africanfuturism Defined” (2019). Karen Lord and Tobias S. Buckell, in turn, edited the anthology Reclaim, Restore, Return: Futurist Tales from the Caribbean (2020), in which Lord’s introduction “Our Sanctuary Sea” outlines the contours of Caribbean futurism through the three titular key words, providing a Caribbean echo piece to Dillon’s influential introduction “Imagining Indigenous Futurism” in Walking the Clouds.These are but a few collections and studies that highlight the ongoing pluralization of futurisms that now culminates in the framework of “CoFuturisms” as outlined in the tour-de-force publication The Routledge Handbook of CoFuturisms (2023), edited by four key scholars in the field, Taryne Jade Taylor, Isiah Lavender III, Grace L. Dillon, and Bodhisattva Chattopadhyay. Based on their respective focus areas, the collection of fifty-nine chapters is structured into four parts, “Indigenous Futurisms,” “Latinx Futurisms,” “Asian, Middle East, and Other Futurisms,” as well as “African and African American Futurisms.” While this might appear as a rather forced and potentially counterproductive grouping at first sight, Taylor’s introduction to the volume and to the notion of CoFuturisms provides the logic for this approach. Framed not only as a movement “within science fiction and fantasy” but also “past the boundaries of speculative fiction,” it is delineated as a range of futurisms by “people of color and Global South Futurisms,” each with “a clearly identifiable movement, mode, aesthetic, and subgenre.” Since each proliferates into various other terms and concepts, no grouping can ultimately do justice to this heterogeneity. Whether as subgenres, movements, modes, or aesthetics observable across a wide spectrum of genres and media whose commonality is discerned by the editors as offering “a vision beyond the white supremacist future” dominating the Global North, or as “an intellectual framework,” CoFuturisms aim for justice and inclusion through critique and witnessing, and they do so by connecting “ethnic specific and regional specific futurisms.”What one can clearly sense here is the avoidance of singular discerning markers and instead an insistence on their plurality, which leaves room for the examination of manifold possible relations, including ambivalences, ambiguities, and contradictions. Rather than a conceptual weakness, this appears to be the very driving force of the framework. Hence, whether a cultural text is placed firmly in a specific context or transgresses common conceptual boundaries that can be marked by smaller geographic terms or ethnic labels seems to lose relevance. Specificity thus is but one dimension through which to analyze these cultural materials, while connections and overlapping themes, interests, and strategies of representation become equally, if not more important. At the same time, the framework is supposed to be able to both maintain and transgress the “shared history” of colonization and imperialism, working toward healing, collaboration, and alternative ways of being. Mapping the main strands of such futurisms, it becomes clear that categories are supposed to overlap and that most cultural works can fit several descriptors. For example, the decision to subsume the Caribbean under Latinx futurisms is based on a notion that “Latinidades” connect to both Indigeneity and Blackness, and the Latinx marker thus is supposed to counter “pervasive anti-Black sentiments” that “foreclose the Black Caribbean from discussions of Latinx America and its diaspora.”Taylor’s introduction—and the collection as a whole—makes clear that the only solution for the classificatory dilemma that appears to be inevitable no matter which umbrella terms are chosen is to instead focus on the textual and cultural dynamics of the respective approaches and texts under discussion. Hence, the decision to favor “CoFuturisms” (derived from Chattopadhyay’s earlier notion of “CoFutures”) rather than “Alternative Futurisms” is based on the notion that this framework does not reduce these dynamics to an oppositional or responsive function and facilitates decolonial options. Conceived as an exercise in “collaborative thinking,” the handbook’s aim is to both “amplify” and “break down” specifics while pushing “past such boundaries and categorizations.”Indeed, while some contributions outline distinct politics or aesthetics, most enter into comparative dialogues, at times in unexpected combinations and variations. Chapters variously offer definitions, overviews, terminological and conceptual debates, community-specific contextualization or comparative approaches, as well as close readings of individual or a range of texts within and across genres and media. Analyzed materials include novels, shorts stories, graphic novels, poetry, video poetry, film, television series, photography and paintings, performance art, protest and artistic movements, as well as music videos.In the first part, “Indigenous Futurisms,” regional variations are frequently mediated by reference to Dillon’s introductory outline of major science-fiction elements in Walking the Clouds, as well as Gerald Vizenor’s notion of “survivance,” refracted for instance through “Pasifikafuturism” (Gina Cole, chapter 5), or “Blackfella futurism as an antipodean offspring of Indigenous futurism” (Mykaela Saunders, chapter 9). From conceptualizations of the “future imaginary” (Jason Edward Lewis, chapter 1) to examinations of “spatial poetics” in “speculative landscapes” (Julia Siepak, chapter 11), critical dialogues within and across chapters provide both place- or culture-specific analyses and wider comparative discussions. Analyses of extractivism or toxicity and biopolitics in cyberpunk and other futuristic genres “reveal the structuring absence of Indigeneity in discussions of chemical risk and exposure” (Stina Attebery, chapter 2). They stand in conversation with other ecological and ethical concerns (examined, e.g., by Conrad Scott, chapter 10, as “Indigenous ecocritical futurisms,” or as “eco-SF” by Patrick B. Sharp, chapter 12) and are also brought to the fore by practices of witnessing or queering (e.g., Channette Romero, chapter 8, on Two-Spirit and Indigiqueer futurisms) as well as emphases on relationality and kinship beyond Western notions of species boundaries. The idea of shaping and reshaping the world through art and storytelling, informing notions as well as visions of the future—whether dystopian (e.g., Graham J. Murphy, chapter 7, on young adult dystopias as “survivance” tales) or hopeful—is at the core of many examinations.Here as in the other parts, some of the most interesting chapters place Indigenous and Afrofuturist or Africanfuturist conceptions in dialogue or draw on materials from different cultural settings (e.g., Arlie Alizzi, chapter 4; Cole, chapter 5). Technological engagements include video poetry as an “expression of both digital activism and visual sovereignty” in a discussion of Ojibwe and Marshall Islander artists’ “Indigenous Futurist digital poetics” (Kasey Jones-Matrona, chapter 6). Most of the chapters in part I draw on one or several of the elements of Indigenous futurisms outlined by Dillon, but just as these are pluralized already, their disparate usages create a wide field of notions and visions. In the dialogue across chapters, land defenders fighting off pipeline development in northern British Columbia are considered Indigenous futurists (Anne Stewart, chapter 13) and ancestral codes are shown to function as “atomized bits of traditional knowledge and Native science” (Blaire Morseau, chapter 14). Practices of resistance and reclamation include quillwork and beadworks, which at times indigenize and subvert iconic popular culture images such as “Baby Yoda” in another form of expressing visual sovereignty (Emily C. Van Alst, chapter 15). Significantly, this part ends with a chapter on Okinawan cinematic and televisual storytelling vis-à-vis Japanese science-fiction genre tropes (Kenrick H. Kamiya-Yoshida, chapter 16), which is not grouped in the section on Asian futurisms but positioned within Indigenous futurisms, highlighting shared concerns against the backdrop of different—yet partially overlapping—histories of colonization. This is one of the instances in which the collection’s strategy and notion of CoFuturisms becomes particularly tangible.The second part comprises “Latinx Futurisms,” understood as including the entire Caribbean. In Reclaim, Restore, Return, Lord and Buckell conceptualize Caribbean futurism in the singular—as opposed to the continuous pluralization of all subgenres or categories in the Handbook of CoFuturisms—as a “practical, results-oriented collaboration of literature, science and policy,” with “reclaiming” being conceived as taking “control of the technology and processes that govern and regulate your daily life,” “restoring” as “both stewardship and self-care, external and internal,” and “returning” as a “mental and physical imperative” in light of the migratory dynamics of the Caribbean.1 Such a framing certainly is compatible with the chapters subsumed under “Latinx Futurisms,” even though most contributions emphasize different aspects. Migrant workers in the United States are discussed in a Mexican frame of reference through the representations of braceros in a 1959 documentary and the science-fiction mockumentary Why Cybaneros? (1997) in comparison to a novel and performance art (Catherine S. Ramírez, chapter 17; Alejandro Morales’s 1992 novel The Rag Doll Plagues is also discussed by Daniel Schreiner, chapter 24). Cross-reading a “Nuyorican” photo series with Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man (1952) in relation to the figure of the “creative technologist,” in turn, offers another cross-genre conversation on (proto-) Afrofuturistic metaphors and aesthetics (Goodwin, chapter 17).Further cross-cultural readings include dialogues between different Indigenous scientific knowledges in North American and African contexts, which facilitate analogies while, in some chapters, tend to lose sight of cultural specificity. Across this section, spiritual practitioners’ “metaphysical technologies” as depicted in a Columbian time-travel television series (Vanessa J. Aguilar, chapter 20) meet with more complex temporal dynamics in an examination of Anthony Joseph’s 2008 novel The African Origin of UFOs (Liam Wilby, chapter 23), as well as the transformative power of “utopic rage” in the context of Nalo Hopkinson’s Caribbean futurism (Cassandra Scherr, chapter 21). What connects many of these chapters is a focus on the decolonial potential of speculative futures, no matter under which label they are discussed. In this way, a productive dialogue between Afrofuturist, Indigenous, and “Chicanafuturism” (Ramírez) indeed becomes possible, with Chicanx futurism in “cyberpunk pedagogical performances” offers a reading of “reversed epistemologies and disidentified bodies” working toward “new forms of society based on a posthuman aesthetic” (Eduardo Barros-Grela, chapter 27; see also Lysa Rivera on “Chicanafuturity,” chapter 30). A short programmatic depiction of Mexican American futurism (David Bowles, chapter 31) adds to the diversification of Latinx futurisms explored in this part.Decolonial options are also explored in a Chilean horror film (Márton Árva, chapter 25) as well as in a broad survey of distinct and overlapping futurist imaginaries within Brazilian science fiction (Vítor Castelõs Gama with Alan de Sá and G. G. Diniz, chapter 26), with a complementary chapter specifying Brazilian Afrofuturism as a social technology connecting earlier phases of activism with the Afrofuturistic movement’s use of performativity and “critical hope” to counter the unfulfilled notion of racial democracy (Patrick Brock, chapter 29). The chapter on “Crossing Merfolk,” in turn, stands out as a detailed study of how African diasporic peoples are centered “in fantastic rituals of fugitivity and refusal,” examined through various iterations of “Aqua-Afrotopia” (Jalondra A. Davis, chapter 28). This chapter could also have been grouped in Part IV, “African and African American Futurisms.” Again, however, it is the strategic mingling and mixing that enables a clearer perspective on overlaps as well as specificities of the many different notions of decolonial futurisms elaborated throughout the Handbook of CoFuturisms. This strategy is brought full circle at the end of Part II with ire’ne lara silva’s observations on the necessity of “transformational narratives” facilitating the “undoing,” “unraveling,” and “unmaking” of the legacies and continued practices of “writing for the white gaze” (chapter 32).The seemingly most incoherent third part of the collection, clustered as “Asian, Middle East, and Other Futurisms,” aims to place reappropriated and relational notions of Sinofuturisms, which reveal contradictory usages of the future in contemporary China (Virginia L. Conn and Gabriele de Seta, chapter 33), in dialogue with Daoist readings of a Chinese novel (Regina Kanyu Wang, chapter 34), “Sino-Fi” web fiction and period drama (Sheng-mei Ma, chapter 40), and Korean American speculative poetry (Claire Stanford, chapter 35; see also Stephen Hong Sohn, chapter 37, on Korean futurism), in addition to several chapters on Indian and Hong Kong science fiction films (Goutam Karmakar and Somasree Sarkar, chapter 38; Kenny K. K. Ng, chapter 39). Here, too, critical engagements with techno-orientalist tropes and stereotypical depictions form a base line that runs through various contributions across different cultural contexts. “Sino-Fi” futurism is shown to be “b(l)inding Chinese subjects to cultural memory from the past and neoimperial soft power into the future” (Ma, chapter 40), which can be further complicated by reading it alongside Euan Auld and Casper Bruun Jensen’s experimental analysis of contemporary Hong Kong as a “still floating, living science fiction” against the backdrop of activism and “Silkpunk,” which aim to “keep alternative futures open” (chapter 44).Different usages of the past are also elaborated in Sami Ahmad Khan’s chapter on the “Golden Past” in Indian Anglophone science fiction, which he positions as being haunted by “indigenous pastism” in the service of Hindutva “reification of politico-religious models of mythological empires,” thus demonstrating the recolonizing potential of futurist imaginaries in the current political climate in India (chapter 42). Dreams of gender equality are pitched against the controlling male gaze in Chinese women’s “heterotopian SF” (Frederike Schneider-Vielsäcker, chapter 41), which can be productively read alongside Sheetala Bhat’s examination of the “Indian woman” in the theater play C Sharp C Blunt (2013), which, via Donna Haraway, questions the nationalist imagination through the “interruptional relations” of “cyborgian futuristic politics” vis-à-vis Hindu patriarchy (chapter 43). Another set of articles examines connections between Arabfuturism and Afrofuturism as well as Africanfuturism in a series of digital paintings (Omar Houssien and Srđan Tunić, chapter 36), and the notion of “critical Gulf Futurism,” which exposes the failures of a fast-paced, hyper-futuristic economic and social transition that invisibilizes the inequalities on which it is built (Shadya Radhi, chapter 45).The last part of the Handbook of CoFuturisms focuses on “African and African American Futurisms.” Interestingly, this phrasing ignores Nnedi Okorafor’s insistence on Africanfuturism as a single word, which again can be explained by the collection’s insistence on pluralization rather than singular definitions. title: Altera Roma: Art and Empire from Mérida to Mexico
abstract: This volume presents a collection of symposium papers originally presented at the Getty Villa in 2010. Grounded in art history, history, and archaeology, the symposium, organized in conjunction with the exhibition The Aztec Pantheon and the Art of Empire, brought together a range of specialists who examined the arts and material cultures of the Romans, Spanish, and Aztecs. Questions concerning imperial organization, expansion, worldview, and social identity, including the roles of monumental architecture, sculpture, and performance in processes of imperial consolidation, guided the case studies presented.Walter Scheidel opens the volume from the point of view of the comparative historian, from which he identifies the common assumptions, methods, and analytical frameworks found in the study of empires. Scheidel underlines that empires are normally studied in relation to five historiographic traditions: the ancient Near East and Mediterranean empires, Islamic empires of the Middle East and India, empires in China and the Eurasian steppes, pre-Columbian formations in the Americas, and European commercial and colonial empires. He adds that a study that includes such seemingly disparate contexts as the Aztec, Spanish, and Roman opens up new avenues for comparative historical analysis.Archaeological remains and the information that they provide regarding imperial ideologies and strategies are a continuous thread in the volume. Jonathan Edmondson looks at the ancient Roman site of Augusta Emerita, known as Mérida, in Spain through the work of humanist Elio Antonio de Nebrija, who wrote about Mérida's history and described monuments at the site. Edmondson observes that Spaniards were expressing interest in Roman ruins just as Spain was commencing its own imperial expansion, an awareness that provided the Spanish with a classical lens through which they could understand and describe the inhabitants of the Americas; it also provided models that they could implement. Similarly, Leonardo López Luján investigates the manners in which the archaeological excavations at Pompeii and Herculaneum informed archaeological interest in the pre-Hispanic cultures of central New Spain in the eighteenth century. He notes that this interest is reflected in the writings of scholars and religious men in the viceroyalty, signaling a significant development given the new value with which the indigenous past was imbued by creoles in their quest for independence.While Emily Umberger looks at the installation of Aztec monuments dedicated to weather deities in imperial provinces as a way of controlling those areas, other authors examine the manners in which elements of Aztec culture were interpreted by Europeans at home and in the Americas. Using the Laocoön as a point of departure, Thomas B. F. Cummins considers how classical and Aztec sculpture were understood in relation to both their original narrative contexts and the sixteenth century when they were discovered. He observes that while Aztec sculpture was being destroyed or buried for depicting demonic idols, pagan classical works were being reclassified as art. Cecelia F. Klein focuses on how accounts of human sacrifice among the Aztecs were visually interpreted by Europeans. She notes that the earliest images of Aztec human sacrifice were based on references to the more familiar Mediterranean world. Illustrations of Aztec ritual practices, associated with evil, cannibalism, and barbarism, were based on images of devil worship, witches, Mongols and Tartars, and bloodthirsty Jews.Along the same lines, Andrew Laird and Guilhem Olivier consider the ways in which classical models were brought to bear in the interpretation of Aztec deities. Although both focus on Bernardino de Sahagún's Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (1575–1577), Laird notes a parallel in the identification of Aztec deities as demons, devils, and false gods with similar approaches in the identification of Greek and Roman gods, while Olivier suggests that comparing Mexican natives to the Greeks and Romans led to granting the original inhabitants of New Spain a prestigious place among civilized peoples. These two chapters, however, overlap to such an extent that they seem redundant.A final approach compares Aztec and Spanish imperial expressions of dominance. Eulogio Guzmán studies the symbolic significance of the Aztec Templo Mayor as a visualization of Mexica politics in relation to the frontispiece of Thomas Hobbes's Leviathan (1651). He suggests that although the Templo Mayor and frontispiece are unrelated there is overlap in the conceptualization and representation of authority across this gulf, but his argument is unconvincing. In contrast, John M. D. Pohl proposes that an underestimated aspect of Hernando Cortés's political strategy was his exploitation of indigenous religious ideology, specifically that surrounding Quetzalcoatl and deity impersonation. He compares Cortés's embracing of indigenous practice in Mexico to Alfonso V of Aragon's triumphal entry into Naples and Alfonso's conscious reference to pagan myth and his new role as divus, parallel invocations of pagan and indigenous myths to consolidate imperial power in the present.As a whole, this volume is an invaluable contribution to the study of the cultural processes following the first encounters between Europeans and indigenous Americans. It captures the complexities characterizing the emergence of the early modern Atlantic world and should thus be of interest to scholars from a range of disciplines.

title: Tying the Threads of Eurasia: Trans-regional Routes and Material Flows in Transcaucasia, Eastern Anatolia and Western Central Asia, c. 3000–1500 BC. By Toby C. Wilkinson. Leiden: Sidestone, 2014. Pp. 406. €49.95
abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeBook ReviewsTying the Threads of Eurasia: Trans-regional Routes and Material Flows in Transcaucasia, Eastern Anatolia and Western Central Asia, c. 3000–1500 BC. By Toby C. Wilkinson. Leiden: Sidestone, 2014. Pp. 406. €49.95Mitchell S RothmanMitchell S RothmanWidener University Search for more articles by this author PDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreThe insight that has directed archaeological research over the past three decades is that the dynamics of development relied on the interaction of peoples, often over great distances. This interaction constituted more than trade; it also included the dissemination of ideologies, population, and technologies. These interactions affected the conditions under which local customs, practices, and organization evolved in many places. For Mesopotamia, this insight is what led Guillermo Algaze to Immanuel Wallerstein’s world-systems theory to explain state origins and development in fourth-millennium-bc Mesopotamia, for example.1In this volume, Toby Wilkinson takes this insight as the basis for a broad and useful analysis of the societies of the Eurasian mountains and highland steppe. His geographical focus is Eastern Anatolia, the South Caucasus, and west-central Asia, although the North Caucasus, Mesopotamia, the Aegean, the Indus, northern China, and Egypt come into the picture to some extent. His time frame is from 3500 to 2000 bc, as reflected in a valuable multi-regional chronological chart in chapter 1. Parenthetically, the continuing problem of nomenclature is highlighted in this crazy quilt of terms applied to the localities in the table. What do terms like Neolithic, Chalcolithic, Bronze, or Iron Age mean across such widely scattered regions?In essence, this book represents a journey over vast spaces and long time periods. As Wilkinson writes, “Trans-Eurasian exchange between west and east Eurasia involved the movements of materials, traditions and technologies (and presumably genes) over gigantic distances and may have begun even before the origins of farming” (p. 23).The first chapter of his quest, “Contexts and Frameworks of Research,” lays out the theoretical history and direction for his study. This is a complex argument that requires one to discuss the meaning of goods in social or cultural spaces, the effects of cross-cultural contact, and the role of the materials both visible (archaeologically recoverable) and invisible (language, ideologies, unrecoverable “goods” like workers, free or slave). He asserts that a “structuralist-interactionist” or “systematic-interactionist” model (p. 28) is best suited to understand the relation of trade to larger cultural changes over space and time. In essence, this approach sees the movement of goods not as external to cultures, but as a kind of vehicle for transformation of core cultural meanings through the societal interaction in the process of trade (as discussed by Arjun Appadurai and others who write about materiality).2 One of his clear influences, in my opinion, was the late Andrew Sherrat. These trade links, according to Wilkinson, form complex networks, each involving different players in different social positions (hierarchical, ideological, commercial, geographical). In this way older, simplistic, descriptive terms like “diffusion” are able to be investigated in more nuanced, frankly processual ways.To this juncture all his points are clearly stated and become apparent in the analysis of materials he presents. More problematic, however, is the last part of chapter 1, “Frameworks for Interpretation,” separated in the volume by clear and well-illustrated sections on the relevant geographical, environmental and chronological frameworks, as well as a section on modes of transportation and a summary of assemblages and sites. At the same time, Wilkinson’s discussion seems to ignore or not be aware of much recent literature and simplifies others’ arguments a bit too much. In its discussion of elements like style and technology, his work relies on terms like chaîne opératoire, techniques du corps, prazeology, skeuomorphism, etc., which are not fully explained. These terms are not woven into his narrative and are not evident in the analysis which follows or in the conclusions, which are materially based.We are in a period when jargon is replacing clear explication; it is ironic that post-processualism, which supposedly is replacing the processualism of the New Archaeology, is guilty of the same obsession with jargon in its early phase. Rather than making an affirmative argument, Wilkinson’s work relies too often on mischaracterizing older schools and setting up straw men to knock down. In fact, at times, in wanting so much to see cross-cultural interaction as the key, I think his analysis ignores the nature of culture change. He writes, “… ethnographic accounts, whilst sometimes comparative, still tend to focus on the local dynamics of technologies within particular cultural contexts. From an archaeological perspective, more interesting is the dynamic flows of technologies and skills in space and time and, potentially, across cultural or geographic boundaries” (p. 58). Evolutionary changes, whether biological or cultural/societal, are ultimately local. How a population within a societally defined space reacts to challenges, and why it adopts exotic goods and ideas may be affected by external factors. However, change happens locally in the same way that selection works on the individual genome but becomes apparent in the distribution of population phenomes. The idea of world-systems theory that these networks create a kind of single culture or society does not match the actual data, nor does it explain what happens when the world system declines or collapses. In that light, Wilkinson and others propose that the highland-lowland trade networks reflected in the Uruk expansion collapsed at the end of the fourth millennium bc, which contradicts his own conclusions that trade increased after 3000 bc.At the end of the first chapter, he defines four largely material goals: methods to identify and understand ancient routes, how to reconstruct the flows of three archaeologically recoverable materials (stones, metal, and textiles), what effects the flow of these materials had on local development, and whether it is possible to verify the existence of a prehistoric Silk Road.The actual analysis begins in chapters 2 and 3, discussing the first of these goals, reconstructing ancient trade routes. He begins with historically attested routes (Roman roads, caravanserais, travelers’ accounts, historical accounts, and modern roads), and then works backwards in time. The assumption he makes here is that there is “route inertia,” that is, the likelihood that modern routes follow the same paths through the landscape as the most ancient ones did. Mostly, this is all solid and worthwhile; however, more attention on the modes of travel might have helped his explication. In rejecting the idea of an ancient Silk Road as more mythological than real, however, his argument ignores the well-documented Khorasan High Road,3 which, in fact, he then discusses briefly in chapter 3. I cannot claim to know the farther eastern part of the route, so on that he may be right, but once one crosses into Iran (and Afghanistan?), the existence of that part of the High Road toward Mesopotamia in the third millennium bc is quite clear. His GIS, “costbased” analysis of possible ancient routes in chapter 3 is interesting and potentially a new tool for analysts.Chapters 4, 5, and 6 follow the patterns in the flows of stone and stone objects, metals, and textiles, respectively. He begins chapter 3 with the case of lapis lazuli. Given that we can clearly demonstrate only one source in Badakhshan, Afghanistan, and know of many instances of its use, often in graves, at the Mesopotamian endpoint and along the route, this is a great case to start with. His analysis assumes—I am not sure it is warranted—that its value is determined by “its ‘resistance to be owned’—i.e. their scarcity, distant origins or field of control” (p. 124). There are many other possible characteristics that convey meaning. For example, gold in ancient Panama was valued not for its rarity or distance from its source, but rather its ability to be formed into complex shapes.Accuracy is important here. In his optional routes one and three, his discussion cites Georgina Herrmann’s excellent first try at making sense of the distribution of lapis lazuli at the end of the fourth millennium,4 including her dating of Tepe Gawra, which, as numerous publications from the late 1990s onward attest, is about five hundred years too late. It is interesting to note that lapis has not been recovered from the Kura-Araxes highland. He asserts later that “colour symbolism and dramatic visual effects” play a major role in lapis, carnelian, and other stones’ social value (p. 156). This is possible, but it is hard to prove. Especially without contemporaneous outside sources like writing, how can we know what attracted ancient peoples? Maybe it was the ease of carving. Plotting the sum of semiprecious stones, obsidian (absent in central Asia), and stone weights provides the clearest results. There were quite different spheres of exchange. There were not established routes along which every commodity traveled.The most highly discussed and most controversial of the book’s topics is metallurgy (chapter 5). Wilkinson begins by returning to the idea that metallurgy is ritualized, that the color of the ores was essential to its earliest exploitation as beads. He then rightly focuses on the sources of copper ores, tin for alloying these metals into bronze, as well as other metals like silver, gold, lead, and iron. He points out that determining which sources the ancients knew is difficult. He then traces the flows of metal objects. His section on Transcaucasia is too broad, combining Arslantepe with the eastern regions and conflating Kura-Araxes cultural-tradition sites with Bedeni and Trialeti ones, which are arguably after the end of the Kura-Araxes.In his most recent article, Antonio Sagona wonders whether metallurgy in the Transcaucasian (in the east, called the Southern Caucasus) region was all that critical.5 My own work at the third-millennium-bc Kura-Araxes site of Shengavit in Armenia has shown a dearth of metal objects. Most metal at Shengavit and elsewhere, as Wilkinson states, was used for items of personal adornment rather than tools. Only after the disappearance of the Kura-Araxes lifestyle and, in most places, of the characteristic Kura-Araxes pottery, are really major increases in the use of metal for tools and everyday items like frying pans and pots documented. The supplies of ores that fueled this increase may also have been enhanced by sources in the Gulf and beyond.Recent trace studies of minerals and ores in southern Mesopotamia show that their sources were from Taurus Mountains, not Transcaucasia. The transfer of copper ores from the Transcaucasus to the North Caucasus Maikop people is well documented, but the importance of metallurgical techniques in Transcaucasia might not be that great. Tracing the routes of metal exchange by pottery style, such as so-called metallic wares in northern Mesopotamia and Namazga V in southern Turkmenia, Wilkinson suggests, may help to define changing metallurgical provinces, as Chernykh et al. define them.6 He further explores the possibility that Kura-Araxes pottery wares were based on metal shapes, although archaeologists recovered few such metal objects before the end of the third millennium, that is, after the Kura-Araxes tradition and its settled lifestyle had largely disappeared. He rightly concludes that “the distance between ore sources stimulated trade, but the manner of the consumption of metals differed on a local and regional level” (p. 222).Chapter 6 discusses an even harder-to-find category of produced goods: textiles. Much of this chapter focuses on areas outside the core focus of the book. Most of the textile patterns are from wall paintings, seals, or pottery. Pins and beads form a second part of his data set. Here, his most important conclusion may not be about the exchange of textiles, but rather about the ethnic, regional, and status differences reflected in cloth patterns and the design of garments.In his concluding chapter 7, he begins by looking at shifting material flows over a series of defined periods (3200–2900 bc, 2900–2600 bc, 2600–2300 bc, 2300–2000 bc, etc.). His research appears to ignore recent research, perhaps out of a desire to correlate flows of raw materials and goods with cultural change. In the 3200–2900 bc section, he writes that the relation between Arslantepe and southern Mesopotamia “was not restricted to imported items from the south, but also—apparently—related forms of social organization” (pp. 290–91). This assertion ignores Marcella Frangipane’s long and well-documented case for local development.7 As I have written,8 these trade contacts may well have offered the local leadership the opportunity for promotion or served as catalysts for change, but contacts do not imply the wholesale imposition of foreign practices. Nor is the inappositely named Royal Tomb of Arslantepe necessarily Kura-Araxes. Frangipane and Giulio Palumbi have questioned whether the black, burnished wares at Arslantepe were even from the east, rather than from Central Anatolia.9 More importantly, Wilkinson’s claim here and later that the Kura-Araxes people were responsible for metals trade is highly questionable. Why, with the Ergani Maden mines so close, would they need Transcaucasian ores? The alloys in the Royal Tomb at Arslantepe are more closely related to Maikop technology.This argument about metals trade and the Kura-Araxes continues in his penultimate section, “Patterns and Processes.” I agree that Kura-Araxes populations, both in the homeland and in the diaspora, were not primarily pastoral nomads, although some groups may well have been. Three of the key claims of his argument, however, simply seem wrong: (1) available data “reflect the complex economy of the 4th and 3rd millennium Kura-Arax communities” (p. 310); (2) “additional mobility was provided to Kura-Arax groups by the integration of the horse at the beginning of the 3rd millennium” (p. 310); and (3) “Research at Sos Höyük, for example, appears to show continued localized ‘sedentism’ into the late 3rd and perhaps early 2nd millennium BC” (p. 314). From this, Wilkinson concludes that the Kura-Araxes economy may have been more similar to Uruk and later urban societies than to the local cultures and societies that preceded it in the Transcaucasus. In fact, however, the Kura-Araxes cultural tradition is marked by relatively small, scattered settlements—compare the six hectares of Shengavit with the two hundred and fifty hectares of contemporary Uruk-Warka. The hallmark of the Uruk culture is the development of authority structures, social stratification, and mass production of goods. There is no evidence of any of these among Kura-Araxes groups. H.-P. Uerpmann’s research on the horse indicates that no true horse was evident in Armenia until the Middle Bronze Age;10 earlier analysts seem to have confused onagers with horses.I have concentrated on what bothered me most, a lack of coherent and applied theory and a real misunderstanding of the Kura-Araxes. However, I do nonetheless want to congratulate Wilkinson. Much here is useful and thoughtful. The breadth of the volume, perhaps a cause of some of the problems I have cataloged, is impressive. In the end, what Wilkinson’s work has provided is a model for how to go forward, albeit with refinements and especially more data. One problem is that we still know amazingly little about the Kura-Araxes cultural tradition. On a minor note, a book so rich in data needs an index. All in all, however, this is a volume worth reading and worth owning. Notes 1 . Guillermo Algaze, The Uruk World System (Chicago, 1993).2 . title: Opening Remarks: Abdul Sheriff on Slaves in Indian Ocean Histories beyond Atlantic and Plural Society Models
abstract: Although I am neither from Africa nor Arabia, I think it is of great significance that the Africa Institute has been established in Sharjah, UAE, with the following vision: “The fact on the ground is that the Arab Gulf region is one of mixed populations, in which cultural exchanges manifested in an impressive variety of processes and patterns pertaining to borrowing and assimilation, forced and voluntary migrations, and adaptive strategies, none of which can be fully understood without incorporating Africa into the analysis.” I have been involved in a similar enterprise at the other end of the Indian Ocean, the Muhammad Alagil Chair in Arabia Asia Studies at the National University of Singapore. The founder, Mr. Alagil of Saudi Arabia, was driven by the vision that the deep trade, religious, and kinship relations between Arabia and Asia needed to be studied and understood; these links were by and large peaceful, in contrast with the conflicts and wars that marked both their relations with the West.I see these two institutions as picking up where the Zanzibar Indian Ocean Research Institute (ZIORI) left off when it sadly closed in 2012. To my mind, the three form a research triangle linking Africa, Arabia, and Asia. I had been surprised and honored to be invited by Professor Abdul Sheriff to its opening conference and join its board in 2008. I had worked on Hadramawt in South Arabia and its diaspora in India and Southeast Asia, but not had the chance to follow in its East African footsteps.Wherever one is positioned around the Indian Ocean, one cannot understand the place without knowing something about its connections with other places around the ocean. Societies on its rim are only partial societies that have been shaped by intercourse with mobile peoples from other partial societies across the water. People in Zanzibar, Sharjah, and Singapore instinctively know this. They know it from their food, languages, families, neighbors, and politics. In particular, the emporium port cities host populations and religions originating from Africa, Arabia, India, the Malay Archipelago, and China in varying combinations and proportions. These are the original plural societies for whom God's words in the Holy Qur'an truly apply: “We have made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another.” In them, diasporas are normal rather than exceptional; they have overlapped, coexisted, partnered, traded, raided, fought, and intermarried over centuries, creating new societies out of oceanic connections. Some have even emerged with their own names, such as Swahilis, Mappilas, and Peranakans; these are only the visible tips of the iceberg.Why is it important to recite yet again the importance of the Indian Ocean and its plural sociology in this conference on race and slavery?It is important because the range of relations and experiences found in this arena have been reduced by a notion of the plural society as one in which different ethnic groups meet only in the marketplace, but do not combine. In J. S. Furnivall's original formulation, plural societyFurnivall, a former Indian Civil Service official in colonial Burma and a Fabian socialist turned pro-native activist, was characterizing Southeast Asia under colonial rule, and his plural society concept was a lament meant to underscore the extent to which extreme marketization under colonial rule had dissolved the range of social ties, and reduced all parties to a subset of their full cultural selves. Even European music had been reduced to that of a marching band in the colonies. His solution, for colonies to become independent nations in which a shared national will could be created, was to be dogged by the presumed fissiparous state of the colonial plural society. Scholars of the Caribbean, such as M. G. Smith, took Furnivall's plural society idea a step further: Conflict was assumed to be inherent to ethnic separation, and the built-in potential for violence could only be contained by a Leviathan state, whether colonial or independent.While many of us have lived and continue to experience the interethnic conflicts that have apparently been built into the postcolonial states from the ground up, those raised in the port-emporia cities of the Indian Ocean, like my hometown Penang Island, have had a more expansive experience of the cultural continuum that belies the reductions of culturally impoverished, racialized plural societies that continue to be milked by national politicians as part of their colonial inheritance.This is where the Indian Ocean, and one of its great, inspiring scholars, Professor Abdul Sheriff, come in. He was lucky to have grown up in Zanzibar, and we are lucky that he has turned his instincts into illuminating research conveyed in very clear analytical prose. In the preface to his masterpiece, Dhow Cultures of the Indian Ocean, he says: “I grew up in Zanzibar, one of the numerous dhow ports skirting the Indian Ocean. Every monsoon, the town was almost transformed by the arrival of the monsoon dhows and sailors from Arabia, the Persian Gulf, India, and Somalia. I therefore became conscious of the intermingling of the peoples of the Indian Ocean which underlay the cosmopolitan character of Zanzibar, of which I was myself a product.”2 In 1964, when he was finishing up his first degree at UCLA, the Zanzibar Revolution exploded. His idealized, if not romantic, experience of an innocent childhood in Zanzibar must have ended with a shock, as the racialized politics of native African versus Arab landowners with wealth built on African slave labor culminated in the massacre of perhaps five thousand Arabs and the exile of perhaps another one hundred thousand at the end of colonial rule. Sheriff was not sure whether he could return home from Los Angeles, or was already in exile.Zanzibar in 1964 seemed to exemplify the sort of plural society Furnivall painted, taken to its logical conclusion of violence when race and class were aligned. How to reconcile this with the very different sort of Indian Ocean plural society Sheriff had grown up knowing in Zanzibar?I believe the tragic gap between the Zanzibar of his childhood and the Zanzibar of his sudden, enforced adulthood in 1964 created a tension that has driven his research trajectory. I suggest that that tension may be conceptualized as the gap between a reduced notion of the plural society as formulated by Furnivall, and an expansive sense of the plural society Sheriff experienced in his Zanzibari childhood. I imagine a range of questions would be thrown up by such a consequential gap. Did Zanzibar change from an expansive to a reduced type of plural society? If so, when did this start to happen, what was the process, who or what was responsible? Or was the problem one of perception through deliberate political mobilization, intellectual misunderstanding, or some combination of the two? Most importantly, a hypothetical: Was it all water under the bridge, or could history be reversed?The way he went about seeking answers to these questions I think is of relevance to the two important themes of this conference: slavery, and the comparison between Indian Ocean and Atlantic cases. Let me try to suggest why.His first major book, Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar: Integration of an East African Commercial Empire into the World Economy, 1770–1873, sought to understand the rise and decline of two classes of economic elites in Zanzibar under the rule of Omani sultans, who were themselves becoming wealthy controlling the flow of exports while navigating superior British power. While English people had previously made enormous profits in the West Indies and North America in agriculture on slave plantations, a new English national consensus arose in the nineteenth century, driven by manufacturing interests, Christian nonconformists, rising professional classes, and new print media, calling for free trade, free competition, free wage labor, denouncing monopoly in all its forms, including over freedom itself, that is, slavery. Adam Smith's moral and economic philosophy said it best. His Wealth of Nations, published the year the United States gained its independence, denounced the Atlantic colonial system of slavery, monopoly, their need for costly organized violence, and the resulting high prices and low volumes. Instead of an oceanic economy of slaves from Africa, working land in America, enabled by capital from England, a return to English land, free English labor, and freely competitive English capital would create an English manufacturing workshop to generate even greater wealth than their lost slave plantations of America, and would be morally superior to boot. Armed with these ideas, British state and commerce swung to the East Indies, employing the new stick of abolition to measure the legitimacy of native polities, transform or take over them, open up import and export markets for Eastern primary resources and British manufactures, and free their internally oppressed.Viewed from Zanzibar, and the western Indian Ocean more broadly, this push came with exaggerated charges against Arabs as pirates and exporters of slaves from East Africa, which underwrote British dhow chasing in Zanzibar waters3 to muscle in on trade in Arab and Indian hands across the western Indian Ocean, and on the Omani sultan's grip on a key funnel through which trade flowed: Zanzibar. In Sheriff's view, while the number of slaves exported by Arab mariners was much smaller than inflated British estimates, the joint action of British restrictions against slave exports, in 1822 and 1845, coupled with the rising international demand for cloves newly planted in Zanzibar, ironically meant an increase in the number of slaves, now redirected from maritime export to work on land in Zanzibari plantations.In short, there was a new turn of Arab economic activity away from oceanic trade toward production on land for export to metropoles using slaves. For a while this generated great surplus wealth for the new class of Arab plantation owners, including the sultan, as clove export prices kept rising as demand outstripped supply, while imported manufactures kept falling in price. When it suited them, the British could close one eye to slavery so long as it was out of sight on plantations, but generating wealth on the market.The larger story for our purposes here is that in reorienting themselves from wide-ranging oceanic trades, which included slaves but only as one part, toward land, in the form of clove plantations worked by even more slaves, Arabs fell into a double historical trap. First, from being wide-ranging maritime traders, even periodic ones, they became identified very visibly as owners of slaves resident in Zanzibar. This rise of a landowning class of Arabs owning African slaves is part of the process of a reduction in the form of the plural society in Zanzibar, aligning owner of land and African slaves with Arab ethnicity. It is also a reduction in perception, as the high visibility of these Arab elites of wealth overshadowed the many Arabs who were poor porters, laborers, and shopkeepers, and descendants of unions with Africans over generations as well. While Sheriff's Marxian idea of a class of land-and-slave owners put Arabs into view within its conceptual frame, he is careful to note that individual Arabs fell in and out of that frame, as did Indians. Second, the move of Arabs from sea to land was also one from a diversified economy to one overly dependent on one sector: slaves producing cloves. They became indebted to Indian moneylenders when clove prices fell, even losing their land to them; and when slavery was totally abolished in 1873, they became impoverished.Sheriff produces a similar view of reduction in terms of the association of Indians with the mercantile class. Many had come from Kutch in Gujarat, poor as British cloth displaced Indian cloth there. They got their start with credits advanced by American traders, using the facility to trade in the interior. The sultan cultivated them as they expanded the reach of his economic hinterland, financing Arabs and Swahilis in the caravan trade for ivory and slaves. The biggest among them in turn came to provide advances to the sultan's treasury as well, as the customs tax farmers for Zanzibar's trade. The complementary relationship between Indian merchant-financiers and the sultan meant that the Indians were becoming indigenized as pillars of Zanzibari polity and society.Overall, the identification of Arabs with land and slave ownership, and Indians with merchant finance, arose from the creation of economic classes that were part and parcel of the political economy of the Zanzibar state. It was a political economy that fed the rich international markets to which British overlordship gave access. In turn it made the sultan and his localized Arab and Indian commercial partners fabulously wealthy for a good number of decades during the nineteenth century. This wealth from a political economy that was based on land products created in gross form a plural society with inordinately visible wealth in two distended sectors with Indian and Arab faces, ivory from the hunt and cloves from plantations, presided over by an Arab-Omani ruler. In the larger scheme of things, they were all merely a subregional, secondary transmission belt that fed a world market run by Englishmen who were the overlords in both money and power, and who had also taken over the oceanic realm. It was the loss of this oceanic realm that reshaped the previously ocean-based plural societies of port-emporia like Zanzibar.In this groundbreaking book, Sheriff made the case eloquently that to understand enslavement of East Africans in nineteenth-century East Africa, and its relation to Arab, Indian, and Islamic lands and peoples, one needed to bring in the Indian Ocean as a foil, or baseline, to gauge the shape and extent of social transformation. Despite the official British cudgel of abolition, slave-making ironically expanded because it was now yoked to a greatly expanded regional production for a world capitalist market. Those conditions of production of slavery were specific to variables of space, time, and circumstance, and could not be generalized to atemporal or longue durée relations between races, religions, or geographical regions.While his first major book studied the reduction of the plural society in the Indian Ocean, his more recent masterpiece, Dhow Cultures of the Indian Ocean, has gone in the opposite direction. Unlike Slaves, Spices and Ivory in Zanzibar, which linked reduction to a turn to the land, Dhow Cultures explicitly embraces and expands the range of plural societies to be found across the Indian Ocean, across a wide space and deep in time, to a rich panoply. Here, slavery is given one chapter as part of the cultural world of the Indian Ocean. Going earlier than the Vasco da Gama period, the Europeans are done away with. Correspondingly, the treatment of slavery here is less tight and more capacious.In a riposte to nineteenth-century Western stereotypes of Islam as central to slaving, Sheriff examines the provisions for the treatment and manumission of slaves in the Qur'an, Hadith, and practice. Islam neither invented nor abolished slavery. He says, “What it tried to do was to ameliorate the conditions through regulations and exhortations on the treatment of slaves, and to provide for numerous ways for a slave to move out of servility.”4 Islam built in a system of manumission that provided a path to freedom and to integration into society. Slave mothers of children with Muslim fathers were freed on the death of their masters. Thirty-four Abbasid caliphs were born of slave mothers who were Berbers, Iranians, Greeks, Turks, and Africans. Wars and disasters generated slaves; there was no one dominant racial axis, such as white and Black, around which people were enslaved. title: Editorial: Insights in ELSI in science and genetics 2024–2025
abstract: Taken together, these contribu ons mark what might be called the governance turn in ELSI: a shi from evalua ng technological consequences to construc ng the ins tu onal architectures through which genomic futures are shaped. This turn has parallels in broader movements toward an cipatory governance and responsible research and innova on, which similarly argue for embedding ethical and social analysis within scien fic prac ce rather than applying it a er the fact.What unites this diverse collec on is a shared recogni on that ELSI is no longer only about iden fying downstream ethical "implica ons" of completed technologies. It is increasingly concerned with designing ins tu ons, measuring public and professional a tudes, an cipa ng future uses, distribu ng responsibility across actors, and engaging the geopoli cal dimensions of genomic governance. In this sense, ELSI is moving from implica ons to infrastructure: from asking what genomic technologies might do to society to designing the ins tu ons through which society governs genomic technologies.Mikami's contribu on to this research topic offers a conceptual hinge for this transi on: ELSI was born within the "reading" paradigm of genomics, organized around ques ons of knowing, predic ng, and disclosing gene c informa on, but the field is now entering a "wri ng" paradigm in which the central challenge is governing the design and synthesis of living systems (Mikami, 2025). If the Human Genome Project inaugurated the ELSI of reading genomes, contemporary biotechnology is demanding an ELSI of wri ng futures.Historically, ELSI scholars have o en been posi oned as interpreters of consequences rather than co-designers of trajectories. The papers in this collec on suggest a different emerging posture: ELSI as an cipatory, par cipatory, and ins tu onally embedded, shi ing from external reflec on on the consequences of genomic knowledge to collabora ve par cipa on in the choices through which genomic futures are designed.That shi frames this editorial.The contribu ons of this research topic cluster around three important ques ons: what shapes public and professional views of emerging gene c and biomedical technologies; who should bear responsibility for governing these technologies over me; and, what values and governance frameworks should guide ELSI as it becomes more global, compara ve, and ins tu onally embedded?1. Publics, professionals, and the specificity of a tudes A large cluster of papers in this issue examines the public and professional a tudes toward genomic and biomedical technologies. Taken together, they demonstrate a finding that is decep vely simple but consequen al for ELSI prac ce: a tudes are not generic. They are shaped by the specific technology under considera on, the cultural and ins tu onal se ng in which it is encountered, the knowledge people bring, the worldviews they hold, and the risks and benefits they perceive (Greenbaum, 2025a). The lesson is that publics do not encounter "genomics" in the abstract. They encounter specific technologies, embedded in par cular histories, ins tu ons, and moral worlds.DuBois et al. survey nearly 5000 U.S. adults on how religious factors shape support for genomic medicine across a range of ac vi es, including postnatal gene c tes ng, storage and sharing of biospecimens and health data, genome edi ng, stem cell therapy and research, prenatal gene c tes ng, and mRNA vaccines (DuBois et al., 2025). The central finding challenges dominant explana ons in science communica on: more strongly than poli cal affilia on, educa on, or generalized ins tu onal trust, specific belief-level and moral-worldview variables, par cularly acceptance of evolu on and moral commitments to health promo on within spiritual communi es, emerge as the strongest predictors of support. Crucially, it is not religious affilia on per se that drives a tudes; the study finds only small differences between religious groups but substan al a tudinal varia on within them. For ELSI scholarship and public engagement, religious iden ty is a poor proxy for moral reasoning: ELSI must a end not only to who people are, but to the interpre ve worlds through which they understand genomic medicine. Melchior et al. complement this picture from a methodological angle (Melchior et al., 2025). By valida ng the Gene c Technologies Ques onnaire for Greek-speaking popula ons, they provide more than a translated instrument: they show what compara ve ELSI increasingly requires. Their findings reinforce the specificity of a tudes, with respondents dis nguishing between conven onal and gene c technologies, gene c tes ng and genome edi ng, and embryo and adult applica ons. These grada ons ma er because they show that publics do not hold a single a tude toward gene cs. Rather, they make differen ated moral judgments across technologies, applica ons, and contexts. As ELSI becomes more compara ve, it will need tools like the GTQ: instruments that can travel across languages and se ngs without collapsing public a tudes into a generic view of gene c technology. Compara ve ELSI cannot simply translate concepts across languages; it must test whether ethical categories travel well across social worlds.Lee, Yoo, and Kim extend the analysis to ar ficial intelligence in healthcare, surveying over 1000 South Korean adults on their awareness and percep ons of AI ethics in health-related contexts, with direct relevance to genomic and health-data governance (Lee, Yoo and Kim, 2025). Their findings reveal a pa ern that recurs across several papers in this issue: high op mism about technological poten al coexists with significant concern about privacy, error, legal ambiguity, and the need for ethics educa on. A large majority of respondents expressed op mism about the posi ve impacts of AI in healthcare, yet concerns about personal informa on disclosure, AI-caused harm, and unclear legal responsibility were substan al. The study demonstrates that ELSI must increasingly engage with AI governance as a domain inseparable from genomic and health-data-driven medicine: as clinical decision-making passes through computa onal systems whose accountability structures remain underdeveloped, accountability must travel with the data.A Japanese study further develops the public a tudes picture. Sawai, Kataoka, and Koike surveyed Japanese adults on brain organoid research and found broad support alongside concerns about unan cipated risks, commercializa on, and personal informa on leakage (Sawai, Kataoka and Koike, 2026). Notably, some concerns (about consciousness or cloning) may reflect misunderstandings, and comprehension scores were posi vely correlated with support. This suggests that science communica on and governance must develop together: informed publics may view emerging research more favorably, but that does not remove the need for oversight.Cummings, Landreville, and Kuzma examine U.S. public a tudes toward natural and gene cally engineered microbiomes in the built environment, finding that topic-specific percep ons, par cularly perceived benefits, risks, and quality-of-life improvements, predict support more strongly than demographic variables (Cummings, Landreville and Kuzma, 2025). Their work exemplifies an RRI-oriented empirical approach in which public perspec ves are treated not as obstacles to innova on but as resources for shaping responsible development. It also expands the scope of ELSI beyond clinical and reproduc ve genomics to the engineered environments in which people live, work, and breathe. Public engagement, the study suggests, should accompany design choices from the outset rather than follow deployment.Soares et al. shi the lens from public a tudes to professional uncertainty (Soares et al., 2026). Their study of Portuguese clinical gene cists managing low-penetrance copy number variants reveals significant disagreement about disclosure prac ces, counseling strategies, and the ethics of prenatal diagnosis and preimplanta on gene c tes ng for low-penetrance copy number variants, whose uncertain penetrance and variable expressivity create clinical and ethical challenges. The resul ng variability in care, what the authors describe as a "postcode lo ery" in which clinical outcomes depend on where a pa ent is seen rather than on the evidence itself, is a failure of distribu ve jus ce within a single na onal system. It also illustrates a point that public-a tude surveys alone cannot capture: genomic uncertainty is not only a challenge for pa ents deciding what to do with ambiguous informa on; it is equally a challenge for professionals who lack consensus about what to recommend.Finally, Shaheen and Ghaly examine gene ciza on in the Gulf Coopera on Council region, a ending to premarital screening, consanguinity, Islamic moral frameworks, family-centered decision-making, s gma, and the interac on of state moderniza on with genomic governance (Shaheen and Ghaly, 2026). This paper is one of the clearest demonstra ons in the issue of why global ELSI cannot simply export Western secular-liberal assump ons into other contexts. In the GCC, genomic technologies are interpreted through dis nc ve religious, familial, legal, and publichealth frameworks that shape their meaning in ways standard survey instruments alone cannot fully capture. Shaheen and Ghaly's analysis broadens the geographic and cultural imagina on of ELSI scholarship and makes a strong case for contextually grounded analysis.More broadly, their paper invites us to view religious legal tradi ons not merely as sources of resistance or constraint, but as sophis cated norma ve systems capable of enriching public reasoning about technological authority, human agency, and ins tu onal responsibility.Taken together, these papers show that ELSI needs be er compara ve tools (shared instruments, coordinated mul -country studies, and theore cal frameworks that travel) but not at the expense of cultural and ins tu onal specificity. The goal is not to fla local moral worlds into a single global metric, but to build methods that allow meaningful comparison while preserving context.A second cluster of papers addresses a temporal problem that runs throughout contemporary genomics: responsibility does not end when a gene c test is performed, a consent form is signed, or a policy is adopted. Knowledge changes. Variant classifica ons are updated. Databases grow. Regulatory environments shi . ELSI governance must therefore develop ins tu onal models for ongoing obliga on, not merely one-me authoriza on.Onstwedder et al. use their 3-I framework (interests, ideas, and ins tu ons) to examine policy considera ons around incidental findings in large-scale genomic research (Onstwedder et al., 2026). Their interview study with Canadian and European stakeholders shows that disagreements over incidental findings are not simply disagreements over ethical principles. They are also disagreements over ins tu onal roles, stakeholder agendas, policy structures, and the distribu on of benefits and burdens. Different jurisdic ons allocate responsibili es differently, not because they hold different values in the abstract, but because their ins tu onal architectures embed those values in different ways. The 3-I framework is valuable precisely because it makes these structural differences visible rather than trea ng policy divergence as a problem to be solved by be er principle-ar cula on alone.Sentell and Zawa address one of the clearest temporal challenges in genomic medicine: variant reclassifica on (Sentell and Zawa , 2025). As genomic knowledge evolves, variants previously classified as benign may be reclassified as pathogenic, or vice versa. But the du es to monitor emerging evidence, ini ate reinterpreta on, communicate updated results, and recontact pa ents remain ethically and legally underdefined. Their perspec ve proposes a shared-responsibility framework that distributes these obliga ons across laboratories, clinicians, pa ents, and health systems. This is a paradigma c example of what the editorial iden fies as the shi from consent-based to governance-based ELSI: the ques on is no longer only whether individuals consented at the beginning of a clinical encounter, but who remains responsible as interpreta ons change and new clinical ac ons become possible. The professional variability documented by Soares et al. is another expression of this governance problem: uncertainty in genomic interpreta on becomes ethically consequen al when ins tu ons lack shared standards for disclosure, counseling, and reproduc ve decision-making (Soares et al., 2026).Peng, Li, and Lei make the governance shi explicit in the domain of biospecimen data (Peng, Li and Lei, 2025). Their paper argues that tradi onal ownership models are inadequate for governing human biomedical data in the Chinese context and proposes custodianship, poten ally implemented through data trusts, as an alterna ve. The urgency of this argument was underscored in 2025 when 23andMe, the direct-to-consumer gene c tes ng company, filed for bankruptcy, poten ally exposing the gene c data of millions of customers and revealing the fragility of governance frameworks that rely on corporate privacy policies rather than durable ins tu onal protec ons. The episode illustrates a broader structural shi : just as the commercializa on of space required new regulatory frameworks when smaller enterprises entered a domain previously governed by and for na onal agencies, the prolifera on of smaller genomic companies capable of assembling vast datasets demands governance architectures that were never designed with such actors in mind (Greenbaum and Gerstein, 2024). The conceptual move from ownership to custodianship reflects a broader trend visible across this collec on: from individual control as the sole governance paradigm toward stewardship, rela onal responsibility, and ins tu onal obliga on. Their analysis also demonstrates that governance models must be adapted to par cular legal, cultural, and poli cal contexts; custodianship takes on different meanings and ins tu onal forms in China, the European Union, and the United States.Genomic governance is increasingly entangled with ques ons of na onal sovereignty, biosecurity, cyberbiosecurity, industrial policy, and cross-border collabora on that extend well beyond the tradi onal ELSI agenda.Song, Liu, and Meng provide a rare empirical window into this entanglement (Song, Liu and Meng, 2025).
