title: On Thinking and Working Through a Pandemic
abstract: There are some things the pandemic didn’t change. I am still interested in doing scholarship; friends and colleagues have said that they are too. More than ever, I acknowledge the presence of the present in my approach to the past, having abandoned any conceit that what was going on around me had nothing to do with my choice of subjects or how I thought about them. Academics are embarrassingly well suited to lockdowns, being introverted by the requirements of their profession and possibly by nature: give us our research notes, books and articles, an internet connection, and a place with a closing door, and we have all we need to write. Even while I was teaching last spring—I am not teaching this fall—the shape of my days didn’t shift much. I had time. Yet other important things did change. A pandemic, even despite the considerable privilege of having a stable job, is limiting. Scholars cannot travel to archives and libraries. Conferences, including SHAFR, were canceled or migrated online, which meant that we lost access to some sessions and—more significantly, in my view—had no chance of the spontaneous conversations in hallways or bars that allow us to catch up with colleagues’ work and spark the best ideas. A pandemic is exhausting. Everyone I know says that it has been harder to think straight while worrying about their health and that of loved ones. Teaching online is tiring. There are reports of people sleeping more, worn out from anxiety or sadness or hours sitting at a screen. And pandemics are distracting. It is all very well to say that we have the resources and the time we need for our scholarship. But there is so much else to think about; as Wordsworth wrote, “the world is too much with us, late and soon.” We are overwashed with bad news, and it has not been possible for me, at least, to stop reading it and listening to it. How can we do our work when we are frightened and angry and cannot trust our national leaders to do anything right? The pandemic has brought lessons that both affirm and challenge my thinking and writing about history. The first of these concerns the role of fear in how people perceive each other, within and across borders. I have long admired the work on emotions of subfield colleagues Frank Costigliola, Barbara Keys, and Melani McAlister, who have described the ways in which American Christian evangelicals instrumentalized a discourse of fear to enhance their pursuit of religious freedom abroad through the deployment of U.S. policy.1 McAlister indicates by her examples that fear can be inspired by what is seen, or known; the Voice of the Martyrs and other groups made videos showing (or strongly hinting at) painful abuses of Christian bodies in order to display the persecution suffered by their co-religionists in Asia. Yet, often it is instead the unseen, the unknown, that inspires more powerful fears. The unwanted penetration or violation of the body by some invisible agent is one of the most basic of human terrors. As Joanna Bourke has argued, “the emotion of fear is fundamentally about the body—its fleshiness and its precariousness.” Fear of possession by spirits or ghosts was largely supplanted following the Enlightenment by dread of “unseen yet harmful microbes and bacteria,” with the assurances of science regarded at first as no more convincing than the promises of exorcist priests during an earlier era.2 My study of sensory encounters between the people of India and the Philippines and representatives of imperial states, British and U.S., confirms Bourke’s claim. Indians and Filipinos recoiled from “western” medicine, the gaze or the touch of a foreigner who promised to prevent them from getting a disease or to cure them of one they already had. Removing the sick to hospitals was tantamount to making them vanish. For their part, Britons, Americans, and other participants in empire worried that tropical pathogens, hidden in the swamps and jungles or (worse, they thought) concealed by dark-skinned bodies, might infect them without warning and thereby sicken or kill them. Hidden disease was identified with its dangerous Asian carrier. The unseen threat required visual manifestation if it was to be confronted. Thus, in matters of bodily safety, race told.3 Fears about COVID-19 are to some extent properly democratic: to viruses, all bodies would seem to look alike, and anyone can get infected. But in truth it hasn’t worked that way. Children are less susceptible than adults to getting sick. People of color—who make up a disproportionate number of essential workers, often live in multi-generational apartments or homes, and frequently lack access to health care—have contracted the disease and died from it well beyond what statistical models alone would suggest.4 And, despite clear evidence that the virus was transmitted to the East Coast of the United States primarily by travelers from Europe, U.S. President Donald Trump and others have insisted on labeling it “the Chinese virus” (“kung flu”) and persist in blaming its spread on the irresponsibility of Chinese hygienic practices and the mendacity of China’s leaders. The result has been an increase in the number of verbal and physical attacks on Asian Americans, including children.5 Thus is fear of a pathogen turned with demoralizing ease to racism—a move historians recognize all too well.6 A second lesson of our experience with the coronavirus, and likely the most obvious to historians of U.S. foreign relations, is the global nature of the pandemic—the very definition of which suggests its worldwide reach and strength. Viruses have no regard for national boundaries. They are carried on bodies that move from place to place, and perhaps even on substances that are touched again and again before they arrive where they are going. (Is there anyone reading this who did not or does not disinfect their hands after bringing in the mail?) In this way, we are reminded that the best work of the current generation of historians also moves fluidly, naturally, across borders. I have returned to scholarship that reminds me of this: Sven Beckert’s book on cotton, Erez Manela’s global history of Wilsonianism, Petra Goedde on international peace movements, Matthew Connelly on world population control, Mary Sarotte’s 1989, and many others.7 I have picked up for the first time accounts of the flu pandemic of 1918.8 The spread of the coronavirus, and even more stories about the effort to find a vaccine to prevent it, remind me of the Hungarian polymath Michael Polanyi’s claim that there exists a “Republic of Science,” an idea captured by Richard Rhodes’s magisterial history of the atomic bomb. Science, according to Polanyi, is by its nature a borderless pursuit. “The authority of scientific opinion remains essentially mutual,” Polanyi wrote. Scientists are meant to share data without regard to national borders, visit each others’ labs, publish in the same journals, and meet at international conferences. The thought that a discovery might be confined to a single nation state or private entity is antithetical to the nature of science.9 Scientists may regard this as an axiom, or may have done so in the past. Governments and pharmaceutical companies do not, so we witness efforts to nationalize the hunt for a coronavirus vaccine. I am of two minds concerning this tension. A vaccine is not a bomb. At this writing, companies, funded by governments and sometimes working with universities, are moving ahead with sizable human trials of vaccines. Their formulas are different, and it seems likely that having a variety of approaches aimed at combatting the virus will serve humanity best. If some efforts fail, it will be good to have others that might work. Immunologists in all labs have some understanding of which sort of vaccine—whole virus, genetic (DNA or RNA), viral vector, protein-based—their rivals are working on, so this is a competition that is to an extent open source. Is it likely that a single, international lab, one (say) based in Geneva and run by the World Health Organization, could have done as well as this less centralized approach? As ever, scientists struggle to balance the claims of their international Republic against those of their employers and political leaders.10 A third lesson of the pandemic that is relevant to my scholarship, past and future, has to do with the importance of culture in understanding the human response to life under the virus. I have long been interested in the role of culture, broadly defined, in shaping U.S. foreign relations. It has seemed to me that we miss something meaningful about the ways in which nations and people interact if we neglect those factors that affect the ideas and feelings policymakers deploy as they work, their values, religious beliefs, emotions, and prejudices concerning especially race and gender, their ways of apprehending others through every bodily sense, their understanding of gesture and language, even their grasp of rituals and symbols, theirs and others. Such factors shape the interests of states: perceptions of national security have something to do with how people imagine borders and read threats. The anthropologist Clifford Geertz has most strongly influenced my thinking on these matters, even as I acknowledge the elusiveness of his definition of culture, which he characterizes, by turns and in one book alone, as “webs of significance” spun by human beings, a “set of control mechanisms—plans, recipes, rules, instructions,” and a “historically transmitted pattern of meanings embodied in symbols, a system of inherited conceptions expressed in symbolic forms by means of which men [sic] communicate, perpetuate, and develop their knowledge about and attitudes toward life.”11 Whatever the perils of wrestling with so elastic a concept, culture nevertheless, in my view, tells us a good deal about the world’s response to the coronavirus. The physician and writer Atul Gawande has made this point. Describing efforts—mostly successful—to prevent the virus from overtaking his hospital, Mass General Brigham, in Boston, and the senior living facility nearby where his mother lives (less success there), Gawande lists a familiar first “four pillars” of effective response: hygiene, screening, distancing, and wearing masks. But the fifth, and “arguably most difficult” pillar to establish, he says, is culture. It is possible, he says, to get people “to focus on safety and freedom; keep me safe and leave me alone.” Those are easy enough to imagine. But what is needed in addition is a cultural (and ethical) shift that involves people understanding that measures they may take will keep others safe. They must affirm values of altruism, of the importance of community as well as individual health.12 Geertz’s social “control mechanisms,” his “recipes,” must in this case be recognized and, if need be, changed. There are indications of both success and failure in the quest to create and sustain a culture of community welfare, and they take me back to the lessons of globalism. Some nations have done far better than others controlling the impact of the virus. In East Asia, where masks are often worn against pollution, seasonal allergies, or other airborne illnesses, governments have managed on the whole to contain the worst ravages of COVID-19. Elsewhere, wearing masks has been stigmatized as cowardly or creepy, and it has been harder to convince people to put them on. (Speculation that East Asians have also been successful at virus containment because they social distance naturally are less persuasive, seemingly sprung from stereotypes about Chinese dynastic fears of conspiracy or Japanese resistance to intimacy. We need to be careful with culture.)13 Those governments that have managed to inspire public trust have on the whole fared better than those inclined to authoritarianism, by system or the personality of their leaders.14 Many believe that it is no accident that governments led by women—Jacinda Ardern (New Zealand), Angela Merkel (Germany), Tsai Ing-wen (Taiwan), and Sanna Marin (Finland)—have managed to contain illness and reduce death.15 It is armchair commentary, perhaps, but it is hard to avoid the conclusion that something about the gender expectations assigned to male and female leaders has made this more than coincidence. The kind of community thinking described by Gawande might just be more common among women, and the empathy required of leaders in times of distress may be more available to those unattached to such masculinist behaviors as supreme self-confidence, posturing, and top-down modeling. There is another lesson, one applicable to the field of history generally rather than to the study of foreign relations alone. That is an appreciation for contingency, the claim that all events, causes of events, and ideas, are conjoined with other events, causes, and ideas. John Lewis Gaddis has written that the fundamental difference between doing history and doing laboratory science is the absence in the first of these of “independent variables.” For historians, all variables are dependent, or as Gaddis puts it, “interdependent.” Everything significant hinges on everything else. That is a prescription for indeterminacy, which is no doubt frustrating to those who seek simple answers to historical questions. (It does not mean that truth is ineffable or nonexistent, just complicated.)16 Through this pandemic, I have been surprised that so many of my colleagues, some of whom are historians, seem to expect certainty where it cannot exist. They were quick to indict university administrators for guessing wrong, however briefly, last spring about whether to send students home immediately and how to move fully to online classes. They demanded to know in early May precisely what the university planned to do in late August. They wanted answers, now—clear-cut ones. As a historian, this seemed to me folly. Historians know better than to think that they can predict the future, having failed, for the most part cheerfully or resignedly, to settle on single explanations for past events. If we cannot agree on how to define the U.S. empire (or even, in some cases, whether the United States was an empire), why it took so long for the United States to intervene militarily in the two world wars, and why the nation went to war in Vietnam at all, how can we be surprised or angry that administrators—at a liberal arts college anyway, men and women much like ourselves, but with somewhat nicer clothes—cannot give us straightforward answers to questions concerning how the university should cope with an unprecedented pandemic, especially when the modes of virus transmission, the role of hard surfaces and aerosols, and the importance of “viral load,” for example, are so poorly understood? Administrators gather evidence and make their best judgments—just as historians do. Yes: there is a lot of money at stake for universities. But to assert that campus decisions are all predicated on money is rather like saying that the reason for everything the United States has done (or not done) in the Middle East over the past century is oil: it’s true, but insufficient as an explanation. This brings me to a final lesson of the pandemic. If historians acknowledge the importance of contingency in confronting the virus, as they acknowledge it in their own approach to research, it must follow that they conduct themselves with humility when they do their scholarship. We live, and work, with uncertainty. “History imbues us with agency and with possibility,” according to Drew Gilpin Faust, the historian and president emerita of Harvard. “But I also derive from history a sense of profound humility—in face of what others have confronted in our differing circumstances but common struggle to chart a path through a challenging world.”17 We are imperfect creatures, able to get things right just so often, and only to the best of our abilities. As David Lowenthal has observed in another context, “it is salutary to be reminded that we are perforce fallible not only epistemically but also personally, subjugated not only to our slippery subject matter but to our slippery selves. To the genre's own insuperable limitations––data that are always selective and never complete; the unbridgeable gulf between actual pasts and any accounts of them; bias stemming from temporal distance, from hindsight, and from narrative needs––we must add, and keep in mind, human frailty.”18 This, for me, is the lesson of living in a pandemic and writing history. The limits of our understanding match the limits imposed on us by the virus; we are necessarily reminded of our vulnerabilities as scholars and human beings. Andrew J. Rotter is Charles A. Dana Chair of History at Colgate University, where he has taught since 1988. He is author most recently of Empires of the Senses: Bodily Encounters in Imperial India and the Philippines (New York, 2019). He is currently writing a book on the cultural approach to U.S. foreign relations history.

title: Introduction: Bernard Shaw’s Ireland: An International Perspective
abstract: In an “interview” in The Evening Sun, 9 December 1911, Bernard Shaw remarked that Ireland “is producing serious men—not merely Irishmen, you understand, for an Irishman is only a parochial man after all, but men in the fullest international as well as the national sense—the wide human sense.”1 Shaw considered himself one of those same “international Irishmen,” though his native identity and strong connection to his homeland was often overshadowed by his international outlook. In many ways, he could be described as an outsider, both in England and in Ireland. He attributed his Irish heritage to shaping him as a person when questioned about it on his ninetieth birthday, stating that it made “him a foreigner in every other country. But the position of a foreigner with complete command of the same language has great advantages. I can take an objective view of England, which no Englishman can. I could not take an objective view of Ireland.”2 He closely followed the Irish political and social scene, writing letters to The Star commenting on Irish affairs from 1888, demonstrating that he was never out of touch with what was happening in Ireland. However, his views were not nationalistic, rather he took a practical approach. Shaw’s opposition to violence and abhorrence of nationalism often put him at odds with those fighting for Irish Independence. While Shaw frequently used the world stage to comment on Ireland and the Irish, many of his peers and critics have misinterpreted Shaw’s global views and tongue-in-cheek satiric mode as an indication that he was anti-Ireland or, at least, indifferent to his homeland and his birthright. This was not the case. He did agree with Home Rule stating that “Ireland must have Home Rule . . . she has a natural right to it.”3 Nonetheless, he cautioned against an Irish insular approach to it stating that “Ireland sulking in a corner by herself is nothing; Ireland with her finger in every pie will gather more than her share of plums.”4 Shaw rejected the traditional boundaries of nationalism, instead preferring to widen his worldview. He stated that “Nationalism stood between Ireland and the light of the world,”5 though he does concede that there is no way around it, it was a necessary route to self-government.His view of the world manifested itself through both his dramatic and nondramatic works from very early on in his writing career. His early plays, with a few exceptions, were all set in different countries, visited at that stage only in his imagination. Rodelle Weintraub charts his use of “faraway places as settings for his plays”6 with his first play Widowers’ Houses set on the Rhine in Germany. Mrs Warren, though set in the English countryside had “business” interests in Europe, while Arms and the Man was set in Bulgaria. Man of Destiny was set in Italy, with the later The Shewing-up of Blanco Posnet set in the American Wild West. Regarding the characters in his dramatic works, Shaw was very taken with the work of Henrik Ibsen, who challenged the conventional forms and favored a realistic, serious, and intellectually rigorous drama that tackled contemporary social issues. Shaw’s book, The Quintessence of Ibsenism, was written in response. His first presentation of these ideas was in answer to a call for papers from the Fabian Society in 1890 on Socialism in Contemporary Literature.7 “Shaw argued th[e] viewpoint . . . in which he shows that these plays had at their heart the struggle of a solitary realist against the philistine majority who are led by idealists.”8 He admired Ibsen’s take on the “unwomanly woman” and the “idealist who was a villain.”9 This is obvious from Shaw’s first play, where the character of Blanche Satorius is everything that countered the ideal presentation of young Victorian women. She is demanding, selfish, and often violent, especially when she does not get her own way. Dr. Harry Trench, her love interest, is an impoverished medical student who comes from an aristocratic background and has no idea how he is financed. As the play progresses, it is revealed that his income is derived from slum landlordism, a fact that he ultimately accepts, despite being morally indignant when it was revealed at the outset that was how Blanche’s father, Satorius, made his fortune. The idealist becomes the villain. This laid the groundwork for the characters in Shaw’s future plays. He was not afraid to show the ugly side of life and humanity. Like Ibsen, he was a proponent of the problem or discussion play, moving toward realism with topics such as the “woman question” and social issues tied to corruption and immorality. “In Ibsen’s problem plays, Shaw detected a challenge to the classic dramatic development wherein discussion became a ‘new technical factor,’”10 a tool which Shaw embraced in his own work. He adapted Ibsen’s international influence and redirected its premise through his own work.Although he did travel to Europe periodically during his time as a music critic, his real engagement with international travel only began in 1898 when he married Charlotte Payne Townshend. They traveled widely, visiting France, Germany, and Italy. He traveled to Sweden where he met the Swedish playwright, August Strindberg, a meeting that had a lasting impression on Shaw. He holidayed on the Dalmatian Coast in 1929, a place he is credited with giving the following description: “On the last day of Creation, God desired to crown His work, and thus created the Kornati Islands out of tears, stars and breath.” He visited the Soviet Union in 1931 and met Joseph Stalin, whom he proclaimed admiration for on his return home, a view that was to cost him popularity during the World War II years. He also took a cruise in 1931, visiting Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Egypt, and, very briefly, Cyprus. The 1930s were Shaw’s most active years traveling, taking a world tour in 1932–33, visiting India, Thailand, Japan, and China, where he met Madame Sun Yat-Sen. That Chinese visit was commemorated in 2014 when President Michael D. Higgins, president of Ireland, visited Shanghai as part of a state visit and spoke at the Sun Yat-Sen Museum.11 Shaw, at the end of that first world tour, visited the United States, landing in San Francisco and visiting Los Angeles. On April 11, 1933, he gave a speech to 3,500 people at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York titled The Future of Political Science that lasted 100 minutes.12 Holroyd maintains the reason that Shaw wanted to give the lecture was “to produce an authentic record of what he was saying.”13 Shaw and Charlotte were to visit the United States briefly again in 1936 in their second and final world tour. They traveled from Southampton to Miami, along the gulf of Panama, stopping next at Honolulu, where they had lunch with Charlie Chaplin, who was later to visit them in their London Whitehall flat. In between the two world tours, Shaw also visited New Zealand in 1934 and South Africa in 1935. There is no doubt that Shaw’s international influence was prolific and far-reaching.This was in part due to his mastery at personal branding. In a time long before internet or social media, Shaw built his persona, GBS. He referred to it in Sixteen Self Sketches as “one of the most successful of my fictions.”14 His works often premiered in the United States before they were produced on a London stage. Of his first ten plays, from 1892 to 1900, the first two, Widowers’ Houses and Mrs. Warren’s Profession, were not produced in England until 1907 and 1905, respectively. Mrs. Warren’s Profession was produced in Connecticut and New York in 1905. Of the other eight, four premiered outside of England, three in the United States and one in Berlin. All were eventually staged in England, and two, Arms and the Man and Ceasar and Cleopatra, were performed in Germany. You Never Can Tell was staged in Kraków. Some of his later “big plays,” like Heartbreak House, Back to Methuselah, and Saint Joan, all premiered in the United States, New York specifically. Shaw’s fame was far reaching. His keen intellect, his approach to social and political issues, and his satirical wit stemmed from his formative years in Ireland. He accredits his education to his time, in part, spent in Torca Cottage in Dublin, which had “commanding views of Dublin Bay from Dalkey Island to Howth Head and of Killiney Bay from the Island to Bray Head, with a vast and ever changing expanse of sea and sky far below and far above. . . . The joy of it has remained with me all my life.”15 Growing up in a musical household and spending a lot of time in the National Gallery of Ireland were the other grounding factors in his education and thinking. These three pillars of his youth in Ireland served to make him the man he became: one who through his drama and his nondramatic writings continues to influence dramatic art and critical thinking. His global achievements are solidified with the award of the 1925 Nobel Prize for Literature and the 1939 Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for adapting his 1912 stage play, Pygmalion. Bob Dylan is the only other person in history to receive both awards. Shaw’s recognition came full circle in 1946 when he was awarded the freedom of Dublin city on his ninetieth birthday. His international presence grounded in his national identity as an Irishman reinforced his global influence and significance.Such was the case in 2024 when we planned our Dublin International Shaw Conference, supported by the International Shaw Society and the Museum of Literature Ireland (MOLI), where the conference took place. It was a lively few days in June with a plethora of papers presented that investigated Shaw’s Irishness and how that translated to a global stage. We had four amazing plenary speakers, the first being the keynote speaker, Nelson O’Ceallaigh Ritschel, and the other plenary speakers were Lagretta Lenker, Dorothy Hadfield, and, finally, Anthony Roche, who closed the proceedings as he did for the 2012 Dublin Shaw conference. The Artists Roundtable hosted by David Clare with the IFTA-nominated and award-winning filmmaker Patricia Kelly and actor/director/producer Michael James Ford ensured an interesting and informative discussion on their work and how it relates to Shaw’s work in examining economic hardship versus privilege with issues related to gender and power within relationships. There was a wonderful production of The Man of Destiny by Limerick’s Goose Chase Theatre Company. Paddy O’Keefe’s Shaw Invites You was a delightful one-man show that explored the man himself and lent great humor to the proceedings. Justine Zapin and Samantha Cade, along with Gavin O’Connor Duffy presented a wonderfully devised production of The Discarded Defence: Shaw’s Rearticulation of Roger Casement which yet again fed into the national/international theme of the conference and will feature in this edition of the SHAW Journal.This special issue celebrates Shaw’s relationship to Ireland and his Irish identity through his marked international perspective. The first three essays center on Bernard Shaw as Irish émigré in London, noting how his initial interactions in London coupled with first professional experiences in Ireland shaped his approach to socialist thought, practice, and playwriting. Peter Gahan’s biographical essay features Shaw as a “young adult” and traces his many interactions with Irish and non-Irish people during his first two decades in London. Gahan’s research uncovers the menagerie of personality the young Irish émigré forged connections with. Some of these associates are well-known in Shaw scholarship, like the eclectic Lady Wilde (who wrote poetry under the name Speranza), Annie Besant, and other prominent Fabians. Others, though, are more surprising, such as Bram Stoker, who Shaw knew as Sir Henry Irving’s theater manager at the Lyceum. These early interactions, Gahan argues, significantly influenced Shaw’s understanding of “what being Irish meant . . . in the Imperial capital in the last quarter of the nineteenth century.”Gahan’s further attention on Shaw’s socialist circle and the evolution of his socialist praxis sets the scene for Eamonn Jordan’s assessment of Widowers’ Houses. Drawing on the work of Mike Savage, Jordan uncovers the “complex interfaces of social, cultural and economic capital” at work in Shaw’s first play, and notes that Shaw’s early experience with impoverished communities as a rent collector in Dublin shaped the socialism in Widowers’ Houses. Effortlessly weaving dramaturgical analysis with a critique of our contemporary capitalist crisis, Jordan’s incisive essay reveals how “uncannily prescient” Shaw was in “his exposure of the machinations of capitalist practices, insider deals and wealth accumulation,” a certainly prompt reappraisal of Shaw’s oft-considered crude melodrama. In the article that follows, Lisa Robertson explores how Shaw’s first Irish play, John Bull’s Other Island, and E. B. Corbett’s novel, A New Amazonia, “engages with the prophetic vision and the dream world in order to offer contemplative space for contemporary political concerns.” Robertson compares each writers’ concern with the imperial policies governing the relationship between England and Ireland and their differing perspectives on how migration shapes ideas of home and belonging, noting how Corbett is primarily motivated by the anti-suffrage movement led by fellow novelist Mary Ward while Shaw stages debates around Irish Home Rule and critiques the cultural nationalism of the Celtic Revival.Though Shaw’s first Irish play was rejected by W. B. Yeats and failed to premiere at Ireland’s National Abbey Theatre in 1904, the next three essays illustrate that Shaw had neither rejected the Irish Dramatic Revival nor had he abandoned his Irish outlook in his aesthetic and political work in decade that followed. Mary Christian finds interesting parallels between the dramatic portrayals of Elizabeth I in Lady Gregory’s The Canavans and Bernard Shaw’s The Dark Lady of the Sonnets. Illustrating that both playwrights had previously used “women as symbols to dramatize the plights of colonized Ireland and the struggle for independence,” Christian illustrates how in both Canavans and The Dark Lady, these Anglo-Irish playwrights accessed Elizabeth’s symbolic personae to proffer indirect commentary on contemporary Irish-English relations. Finding links between the suffrage movements in Ireland and England and highlighting the precarious position of the women’s movement between suffrage and socialism, Marie Hewelt’s essay investigates how Shaw’s Pygmalion confronts the contradictions of social class within and surrounding the twentieth-century women’s movement. Providing important context for Shaw’s engagement with the “Woman Question” and challenging received narratives of Charlotte Shaw, Dorothy Hadfield’s important research reveals Charlotte was neither “mere echo” of her husband nor was her “main achievement . . . eliminating domestic distractions so that her husband could focus on his important work.” Accessing newly available archival sources “to uncover the ways that Charlotte demonstrated her own strong commitment to feminism and Irish independence,” Hadfield lays important ground for further study of Shaw’s better half.Charlotte Shaw’s commitment to Irish Independence, Hadfield’s essay proves, influenced her husband’s engagement with Ireland as she moved toward independence. Complicating Ireland’s decolonization was the onset on the first World War, and Shaw’s struggle to advocate on behalf of his native countrymen and maintain his antiwar position in global politics motivate the subject of the next two pieces. Justine Zapin and Samantha Cade’s Verbatim Theatre piece, The Discarded Defence: Shaw’s Rearticulation of Roger Casement, illustrates Shaw’s oft-overlooked incursion into the project of Irish independence, and the transcript of a post-show talk-back highlights how archival sources can be mined for creative outputs. The executions of Sir Roger Casement and the other martyrs of the 1916 Rising become a crucial feature of Irish cultural memory, as Arthur Togores explores in his essay on Shaw’s Saint Joan and Sean O’Casey’s The Shadow of a Gunman. Comparing the two plays, Togores argues convincingly that both plays access the plot and spectacle of martyrdom “to subvert the hegemonic discourse of the nation-in-creation as regards to the place of women” within it.Audrey McNamara’s commemorative tribute to Shaw’s Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925 leads into the final two essays on Shaw and his lasting impact on London theater. Nelson O’Ceallaigh Ritschel deftly navigates the dense archive to highlight how “the 1920s London theater not only resurrected Shaw’s reputation from whatever effects lingered from his war journalism in London, it was also a theater that helped establish Shaw’s full and lasting reputation, on all theatrical levels, as a dramatist.” Deborah Payne continues on this line, tracing how Shaw’s influence on the development of theater in London continued far beyond the 1920s. With beautiful prose and perceptive insight, Payne illustrates how—by the Second World War—Shaw was no longer seen as the perpetual thorn in the side of the Lord Chamberlain but an exemplar theatrical talent and a bastion of playwriting expertise. The discussions engaged within the special issue Shaw’s and him as not merely an Irishman but a man in the international as well as the wide human

title: Contrasting Depictions in 1920s Italian and British Colonial Missionary Documentaries
abstract: the constructions of colonial dynamics in two Catholic missionary films, one Italian and one British, illuminate the respective colonial powers’ contrasting agendas in the 1920s. The Italian documentary Italy in Eritrea and the Catholic Missions (Italia in Eritrea e il ruolo delle missioni, 1922) features Indigenous people, local customs, and Catholic missionaries from the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin. This film presents the colonized and colonizing people in ways that differ sharply from another Catholic missionary film from the same period, the British Mill Hill Fathers Shed Light on the Dark Places of Earth (1920), which features footage of the British colonizers in Uganda. Using sociocultural interpretation as well as a careful look at the images and their denotations, this article shows that the differences in these films mirror the divergent strategies of Italian and British colonial rule in the early twentieth century.Both documentaries were produced by Catholic missionary groups. Italy in Eritrea and the Catholic Missions was filmed in Massawa and other cities in Eritrea. The Capuchins had played a key role in the Christianization of Eritrea. In 1894, the Capuchin father Michele da Carbonara was the first apostolic prefect of the Italian colony of Eritrea, and he influenced substantially the development of later missionary activities. The British film Mill Hill Fathers Shed Light on the Dark Places of Earth was produced by the St. Joseph's Missionary Society of Mill Hill and shot in Kampala, Buganda. When the St. Joseph's Missionary Society of Mill Hill arrived in Kampala and established its station in 1895, Buganda was still an independent kingdom. Five years later, it became a province of the British Uganda Protectorate.Analyzing cultural production in the form of missionary documentaries during colonialism in the 1920s from a comparative view allows for a deeper understanding of the impact religious institutions had in the construction of “colonial subjects.” Missionaries’ difficulty with local languages made images more amenable as a medium to communicate with colonized “children” or “pupils,” as the Indigenous people were called. The missionary documentaries had multiple functions, including the “education” of Eritreans to colonial ways of life and, primarily, the need to raise funds for the missions.Italian and postcolonial studies have been moving toward transnational and comparative perspectives. However, scholarship pertaining to Italian imperialism and colonial rule remains mostly rooted in a nation-state framework, with a few exceptions that compare Italian and German colonial rules. This article's comparative analysis of how Italian and British religious institutions dealt with local communities under colonial rule enhances understanding of what the “civilizing mission” signified in the two European countries. The comparative research thus breaks new ground that makes the respective social contexts emerge more clearly.To Italian Catholic missionaries, the idea of educating the colonized locals was central to their work and ideals, while the purpose of the British Catholic mission was different. The British missionaries’ aim was a civilizing undertaking. To put it in their own words, the goal was, as the title goes, “to shed light” on the colonized people who resided in what the colonizers saw as spiritual darkness. Educating and civilizing are divergent goals of missionary work. Analysis of commonalities and differences in the two Catholic films illuminates the type of work missionaries initiated in their respective colonized communities, and it provides an answer to the question, how did colonialism and proselytism contrast and compare in different colonial settings?This study analyzes the selected documentary films in relation to several questions. What did the respective colonial governments offer by using images to transmit their sociocultural ideas, civic understanding, or rule of law? What was gained from using documentary films in the colonial expedition? How might viewers understand the underlying colonial rhetoric informing the films’ images? Building on Clifford Geertz's conception of “controlled comparison,” this study uses a tightly constructed approach in selecting films that have certain overt similarities. Another foundation is the work of anthropologist Lloyd Fallers, whose ethnographic study of the Buganda (a Bantu kingdom in Uganda) examines the idea of “primordial loyalty” (Fallers 4). This article also builds on the research of Maria Francesca Piredda, which analyzes Catholic cinema and argues that “missionary films are a phenomenon which has been linked to the official use of images by the Catholic Church from its origins until now” (Piredda 214). Missionary films from the 1920s were generally screened for their national Italian and British audiences, who gained a specific, projected idea of the Indigenous cultures. This study expands on Piredda's work to focus on the similarities and differences in the portrayal of colonized individuals in the two case-study films and to link prevailing anthropological and ethnographic frameworks to the colonial cultural production by Italian and British missionaries from the period.Relatively few studies have examined Italian and British colonialism or cultural production from a comparative view, whereas British imperialism has long been the focus of comparative history studies. Among the most recent works, that of James R. Fichter deserves special mention; he argues that British and French colonial empires “were mutually constructed,” such as in their engagement with Islam during the Hajj pilgrimage period, in how they shared control over the Mediterranean Sea, Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and South China Sea, and in how they approached their de-colonization processes (Fichter 60). Similarly, Robert Aldrich's study considers the mutual aspects of British and French “indirect rule”—for instance, in the deposition of native monarchs in Asia and Africa. Aldrich argues that even when colonizers impoverished and destabilized local sovereigns, they could not erase the memory of monarchism in national identity, anticolonial campaigns, and the heritage exiles left behind. The collection edited by Nadine Meouchy and Peter Sluglett features essays on the political and cultural policies of British and French mandates in the Middle East and compares their applications and effects.Studies exploring Italian and British colonial rules from a visual perspective are rare, whereas numerous works have explored British and French colonialism from a comparative perspective. Although Italian colonial experiences are abundantly investigated by scholars, it is not clear why there is academic hesitation to use the Italian colonial case as an example for comparative work. Perhaps the divergent colonial rules employed by France and Italy make comparative studies more challenging. For example, Italy's direct rule approach framed colonial territories as an overseas projection of the national administration. During the empire (1936–41), there was a policy of totalitarian subjection, and Italy did not give importance to the study or preservation of Indigenous cultures. However, before that time, in the liberal era beginning in 1882, there had been a different approach to colonialism. Research by anthropologist Gianni Dore has shown that some Italian officers studied Indigenous culture during the years preceding the invasion of Ethiopia in 1936. For instance, Dore details the work of officer Alberto Pollera (1873–1939), a self-made ethnographer who produced several ethnographic works on Eritrea between 1902 and 1922 that were focused on the so-called customary laws.In addition, divergent scholarly views on the impact of Italian colonialism on Eritrean society raise crucial issues that call for further investigation. One line of research that informs the present study is Tekeste Negash's disagreement with Taddia's findings. Negash states that Taddia has argued without sufficient evidence that Italian colonial rule “brought profound changes to Eritrean society” (Taddia 40). Negash explains, “My main contention with Taddia lies . . . in the problem of assessing the intensity of colonial impact on Eritrean society” (Negash 19). According to Negash, Italy's initial “native” policy considered “the rural nature of the colony and the preservation of Eritrean social organizations” (22). Negash finds that from 1907 until 1932, Italian colonial policies “avoided a drastic reorganization of Eritrean society and economy because of the new economic role assigned to Eritrea” (23).Negash identifies 1932 as a turning point in Italian colonialism; that was the year when preparations for the invasion of Ethiopia began, and the so-called first-born colony of Eritrea assumed greater strategic importance. The political stability necessary for the development of Eritrea's economy in the earlier phases of colonialism was no longer the priority from 1932 onward, with new economic and social strategies implemented to prepare for the war. Historian Lucia Ceci has proposed another periodization, stressing that the period between 1935 and 1938 saw significant changes to the administrative system and ideology of fascist Italy. title: Risk Factors Related to Mobile Phones Use among Higher Education Students in Kuwait: Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Introduction Mobile phones have transformed global communication and information access, leading to profound changes in how people interact and share knowledge. Their swift integration into everyday life has provided clear benefits across many areas of society [1]. In education, mobile phones offer the ability to enrich learning, promote collaboration between students and teachers, and provide flexibility in managing coursework [2,3]. This easy access allows students to connect with classmates, tap into learning resources, and engage with academic support systems, thus fostering a more dynamic educational experience [4]. Nonetheless, the pervasive use of mobile phones has also raised concerns regarding potential negative effects on both physical and mental health [5]. Research has increasingly examined the link between mobile phone usage and various health issues, such as headaches, sleep problems, ear pain, eye strain, and difficulties with concentration [5-7]. Research indicates that both the electromagnetic radiation emitted by mobile phones and the behavioral habits associated with their use may contribute to these adverse effects [8]. While exposure to electromagnetic radiation typically falls within established safety thresholds, ongoing discussions persist regarding potential long-term health consequences warranting further examination [8-10]. Extended engagement with mobile devices for activities like reading or watching videos at close range can induce eye strain and visual fatigue, commonly termed "Computer Vision Syndrome" [11]. Moreover, studies have investigated the link between mobile phone usage patterns and sleep quality, suggesting that late-night usage and the blue light emitted from screens may disrupt natural sleep cycles, affecting alertness and overall well-being [12,13]. Excessive mobile phone use has also been associated with a potential risk of addiction, particularly among younger individuals [14]. This addiction can lead to neglect of essential routines, academic responsibilities, and in-person social interactions, negatively impacting users' mental health [15]. The examination of potential health risks from mobile phone usage has become a pressing concern, particularly among student populations. Young adults, who are among the most active users of mobile devices, often spend extensive time on their phones for several reasons, including academic work, social interactions, and entertainment [14]. This sustained usage may increase their vulnerability to the adverse effects linked with mobile phone overuse. Research conducted with university students in multiple countries has shown correlations between prolonged phone use and physical issues such as musculoskeletal pain, eye strain, headaches, and sleep disturbances [16-18]. Additionally, excessive mobile phone use can lead to psychological effects like increased distraction, reduced focus, and problematic internet habits, which are particularly concerning within an academic setting where sustained attention and focus are crucial. While research on the relationship between mobile phones and health is growing, it has primarily focused on Western industrialized nations, making the generalization of findings to other regions with different usage patterns and cultural contexts challenging. Specifically, in the Middle East, the topic of the effects of mobile phone use, particularly among students, has not yet received sufficiently in-depth investigation. This lack of research extends to the State of Kuwait, where mobile phone penetration is significantly high [19]. The country is particularly relevant for deeper inquiry due to its young population and rapidly developing higher education sector [20]. Understanding the risk factors associated with mobile phone use, the prevalence of health complaints, and the possible impacts on higher education students in Kuwait is crucial for developing appropriate public health guidelines and educational interventions. Current research remains insufficient to fully understand the health complexities tied into the intensive use of mobile phones, particularly within this specific sociocultural context. A closer examination of the relationship between mobile phone usage patterns, demographic factors, and health complaints among students in Kuwait is therefore warranted. This study intends to bridge the existing knowledge gap by conducting a detailed cross-sectional analysis of the risk factors related to mobile phone usage and their impact on the health of university students in Kuwait. The primary goal is to examine how different variables—such as mobile phone usage patterns, demographic details, and existing health conditions—might be connected to various health issues commonly associated with mobile phone use. To achieve this, the study will focus on answering key research questions like: RQ1: How common are specific health issues among higher education students in Kuwait? RQ2: Do demographic factors affect the frequency of health complaints related to mobile phone use? RQ3: What is the relationship between mobile phone usage patterns and reported health issues? Literature Review This literature review explores how mobile phone use shapes higher education experience, focusing on potential health consequences. It examines patterns of student usage, investigating links between use and both physiological and psychological effects. The review pays close attention to studies exploring how factors like demographics or specific habits might make some students more susceptible to health concerns. Particular interest is given to research conducted within Kuwait or the greater Middle East. This analysis will surface key trends, pinpoint knowledge gaps, and provide a durable foundation for the present cross-sectional study. This study delves into risk factors linked to mobile phone use among higher education students in Kuwait. Patterns of Mobile Phone Use among Higher Education Students Research into university student mobile phone usage reveals an innate interrelationship between technology, individual purpose, and the broader social environment. Studies across Kuwait, Oman, and Türkiye illustrate both shared habits and subtle differences in how students use these devices within and outside of the classroom [21,22]. One universal theme is the smartphone's dominance over simpler phones. This mirrors a wider trend, opening doors to constant connectivity, effortless multitasking, and an ever-growing range of applications vital for the modern university experience [23,24]. Studies within the Gulf region offer a window into how Kuwaiti students interact with mobile phones. In Kuwait, research shows a clear pattern where students use their smartphones most heavily at home, but also while traveling, on campus, and during leisure time [25]. This paints a picture of the mobile phone's deep integration into the fabric of students' lives, effortlessly spanning both work and relaxation. Alzougool and AlMansour's (2017) findings also illustrate the phone's place in formal education which is Kuwaiti students extensively use them to access learning systems, check exam dates, and complete other university tasks. This underscores the growing importance of mobile devices as tools for academic success [25]. Furthermore, research from the Middle East reveals how mobile phone usage adapts to modern technologies and shifting generational tastes. Belwal et al.'s (2022) study in Oman tracked a marked decline in Nokia's once-unrivaled popularity, with Apple and Samsung dominating the market [23]. This trend mirrors global smartphone advancements and highlights young users' preference for feature-rich devices. Interestingly, this study also found that students are becoming less dependent on parents for phone subscriptions. This suggests a connection between growing financial autonomy and greater individual phone ownership – a shift that influences how extensively young people use their mobiles. Atas and Çelik's (2019) cross-sectional study of Turkish university students offers a valuable comparison point to those conducted in Kuwait and Oman [22]. Their work aligns with regional findings of heavy smartphone reliance, with students averaging five hours of daily use, concentrated in evening and nighttime hours. Mirroring trends in the Gulf region [21,23], this study reinforces the dominance of social media and messaging apps in student engagement. Across Türkiye, Kuwait, and Oman, behaviors like texting, web searches, and frequent device checks underscore a pattern of deeply integrated smartphone usage. Students wield their smartphones for a multitude of reasons, hinting at how these devices influence both their studies and personal lives. Studies like Alzougool and AlMansour's (2017) from Kuwait show social networking dominates smartphone use, a trend seen globally by the popularity of chat and social media apps [25]. While this digital connection offers clear benefits, research like Kaysi et al.'s (2021) reveals a puzzling gap that despite their constant presence, smartphones remain underutilized as deliberate learning tools [26]. This suggests a significant opportunity to thoughtfully integrate smartphones into educational strategies, potentially unlocking new avenues for student success. Research consistently shows that demographic factors significantly shape how students use mobile phones for learning. In Kuwait, studies reveal that gender, academic major, nationality, age, and level of study can all influence these patterns [25]. Likewise, in Oman, male students tend to use a wider array of mobile features and apps with greater frequency than their female peers [23]. These findings make it clear that understanding the health impacts of mobile phones means considering how demographics might drive both the amount of time spent on devices and the types of activities students engage in. Previous research on mobile phone usage often relied on self-reports, which can be unreliable. Kaysi et al.'s (2021) study takes a groundbreaking approach by directly tracking smartphone usage with an app [26]. Their results are concerning, showing that university students in their sample used their phones for an average of 317 minutes daily. Crucially, the study's qualitative findings show this is not just about time spent. Students report physical issues and struggle to concentrate on their studies – a clear indication their phone habits are causing significant harm. Health Effects Associated with Mobile Phones Intensive research explores the connection between mobile phone use and potential health risks, especially related to the brain, sleep patterns, and eyesight. A central question concerns the biological impact of electromagnetic radiation (EMR) emitted by these devices [8]. Malik's analysis highlights how non-ionizing radiofrequency waves may interact with human tissue. This raises concerns about changes in nerve cell activity, metabolism, chemical balance within the brain, and even the potential for brain tumors [8]. While phone manufacturers strive to limit EMR exposure, the long-term effects of frequent and prolonged phone use remain a significant point of discussion within the scientific community. Deniz et al. (2017) added important insight by focusing on the hippocampus, a brain region crucial for memory formation [10]. Their cross-sectional study of female medical students revealed an intriguing finding: hippocampal volume and structure seemed unaffected by phone usage levels. However, those with higher mobile phone exposure demonstrated decreased performance on attention-demanding tasks. This suggests that EMR might subtly influence cognitive processes like concentration, even if it does not cause overt changes in brain structure [10]. Excessive smartphone use goes far beyond the question of screen time. It is increasingly linked to a troubling range of physical and mental health risks. Wacks and Weinstein's (2021) review offers a stark picture that depression, anxiety, substance abuse, impulsive behaviors, and sleep problems all appear more common in those with heavy phone use [5]. Even the structure of the brain may be altered. Young people, with their developing brains and social lives, seem particularly vulnerable to the negative impact of unregulated smartphone engagement. Ratan et al.'s (2022) investigation of smartphone addiction (SA) among young Bangladeshis reveals troubling findings [6]. Their study found that a significant portion of the young adult population (61.4%) exhibits addictive smartphone behaviors. This addiction is not without consequences. SA directly correlates with poorer physical health, including insomnia and obesity. It also increases the likelihood of mental health struggles like anxiety and depression. These results highlight the urgent need for interventions that promote balanced and healthy relationships with technology. The way students use their smartphones at bedtime is a growing concern and with good reason. Research by Elsheikh et al. (2023) reveals that bedtime phone use is shockingly common among medical students, and it comes at a cost [12]. Students who cannot put their phones down struggle to fall asleep, stay asleep, and get enough sleep overall. This isn't just inconvenient, but it directly harms their academic performance. Beyond sleep itself, studies like Falkenberg et al. (2020) point to a diverse set of worries [17]. Even students with healthy eyes can end up with headaches, stiff necks, and eye strain when they use their phones too much, and too close to their faces. Guiding students towards healthier screen habits is necessary – for better sleep, better grades, and better overall well-being. Intriguingly, some studies offer an alternative perspective on the presumed negative health impacts of mobile phones. In their analysis of the Ravansar non-communicable diseases (RaNCD) cohort study, Amiri et al. (2022) discovered a surprising negative correlation between blood pressure and mobile phone use in women [27]. Although these findings require further investigation, the researchers hypothesize that increased mobile phone usage may facilitate stress reduction and stronger social bonds, potentially leading to improved cardiovascular health. This hints at the possibility of unanticipated benefits stemming from our ubiquitous mobile devices. Risk Factors for Mobile Phone-Related Health Effects Numerous studies have explored the factors that make individuals more prone to the detrimental health effects of mobile phone use. For instance, Thomée et al.'s (2011) insightful study of young adults reveals a vital connection between mental health and the psychosocial dimensions of mobile phone usage [28]. The study found that high-frequency use was significant, but even more influential were qualitative factors such as the stress of constant availability, the perception of overuse, and the pressure to always be connected. Crucially, these psychosocial risks continued to predict stress, poor sleep, and depressive symptoms even after one year, highlighting the lasting impact of our attitudes towards mobile devices on our well-being [28]. Wacks and Weinstein's (2021) extensive research solidify the troubling link between excessive smartphone use and numerous physical and mental health concerns [5]. Their work revealed that women, and individuals who are highly focused on their phones, tend to display more addictive behaviors. Furthermore, certain usage patterns – like intensive social media engagement – were connected to heightened impulsiveness, lowered self-esteem, and disrupted sleep. These findings underscore the several ways smartphone habits, personal factors, and potential long-term health risks may tragically intertwine. Studies on the connections between screen time and health problems consistently highlight the adverse impact of specific usage patterns. Nakshine et al.'s (2022) review outlines the detrimental effects of excessive screen time, including sleep disruption, increased risks of obesity and cardiovascular disease, and worsened symptoms of depression and anxiety [29]. A primary concern is the way blue light from screens suppresses melatonin production, particularly at night, leading to a cascade of negative consequences for sleep and overall well-being [29]. Smartphones in the bedroom compound the issue, with notifications disrupting sleep and shortening its duration. Csibi et al.'s (2021) study on problematic smartphone use highlights the significant disparities in vulnerability across different age groups [30]. Young adults (20-34 years) emerge as particularly susceptible, scoring highly on addiction measures. This is likely influenced by an intense focus on their devices, alongside a reliance on smartphones for emotional regulation. Concerningly, younger children also exhibit risk factors, underlining the importance of early and sustained intervention. These findings emphasize the need for tailored approaches that safeguard against the potential long-term health impacts of excessive smartphone engagement, considering the unique risk profiles of each developmental stage. Chen et al.'s (2017) research into smartphone addiction among Chinese college students highlights a concerning link between specific app usage patterns and mental health risks [31]. Their study suggests gender plays a distinct role where males who frequently use game apps and females who engage heavily with multimedia and social networking apps appear more susceptible to addiction. This finding underscores the need for targeted interventions that address the unique ways smartphone use can become problematic. Furthermore, the study establishes a strong correlation between smartphone addiction and conditions like anxiety, depression, and poor sleep quality, affecting both genders. The research thus far consistently highlights that prolonged mobile phone use, the presence of the phone in bedrooms, nighttime screen exposure, and emotionally driven usage patterns all elevate the risk of sleep disturbances. Sleep problems appear to be a crucial factor that could link mobile phone use with a cascade of other negative health outcomes, spanning from mental well-being and cognitive function to obesity and cardiovascular disease [5,29]. Furthermore, several studies emphasize that the psychosocial aspects of mobile phone use are integral to understanding addiction and adverse health effects. Perceived demands on availability and concerns over accessibility can lead to heightened stress responses related to mobile phones, which themselves become risk factors for mental health concerns [28]. Importantly, demographic factors such as gender and age further compound these risks, requiring both tailored support and awareness campaigns for different population groups. The Kuwaiti Context Kuwait presents a compelling context in which to investigate the relationship between mobile phone use and health concerns. With remarkably high mobile phone penetration rates and rapid social change, Kuwait exemplifies how mobile phones become deeply embedded in daily life. Al-Hunaiyyan and AlHajri's (2018) study reveals an enthusiastic embrace of mobile technology amongst instructors at the College of Business Studies [21]. This openness towards integrating mobile devices into work and educational processes highlights a broader societal trend towards technological uptake. Furthermore, Al-Hunaiyyan et al.'s (2018) work with both students and instructors across higher education institutions confirms that positive perceptions of mobile learning (m-learning) and familiarity with mobile applications are widespread [21]. This receptiveness to integrating mobile devices with learning opens avenues for exploration into the health impacts of such usage. In Kuwait, while mobile devices offer clear educational and social potential, it is crucial to consider how cultural norms may uniquely shape their use compared to the West. Al-Hunaiyyan et al.'s (2018) work highlights a friction between connectivity's advantages and the desire to maintain personal space and privacy [21]. This suggests that mobile phones, while increasingly ubiquitous, could potentially conflict with established expectations around social interaction and personal boundaries within Kuwaiti society. Exploring whether these tensions lead to stress or anxiety around mobile phone use would be a valuable direction for future research. Research examining health perceptions of mobile phones in Kuwait provides important clues about key concerns. Buabbas et al.'s (2021) qualitative work with parents highlights an understanding of the health risks linked to children's overuse of smartphones [32]. Parents were primarily worried about physical issues like headaches and eye strain and behavioral changes such as anger and addiction. These findings mirror similar anxieties about mobile phone use voiced by parents and adults across diverse cultures. This suggests that a feeling of unease about technology's influence on health and well-being may be a broadly shared phenomenon, even in areas where mobile phone use is quite common. Alqallaf's (2022) study offers a nuanced exploration of smartphone addiction among Kuwaiti youth, pinpointing its social and psychological underpinnings [33]. The research underscores a link between addiction, struggles with self-efficacy, and potential friction within both the individual and their family unit. Loneliness did not surface as a major factor.
